channel.title: AI Native Engine × AI Rendering 日报
channel.description: 每日精选：AI 原生引擎 / AI 渲染 / 游戏引擎 / 图形学（全文 + 中文导读）

item.title: 引擎继续跑仿真、渲染交给模型：AlayaRenderer-Flash 吃 G-buffer 出画面，单卡 31 FPS、四步出图 ｜ AlayaRenderer-Flash: Generative World Renderer at the Speed of Play
item.description:
一句话：G-buffer 当契约：albedo/depth/normal/roughness 进去，带风格的 RGB 出来，30 FPS 完整循环。

要点：

  • 分工唯一明确：引擎继续仿真并导出 G-buffer（albedo、depth、metallic、normal、roughness），渲染器把它变成 RGB 帧，风格由一句文本提示决定，速度按播放速率
  • 三项工程手段：自回归 + 长/中/短三级压缩 latent 历史（可无限流式）、从 50 步 teacher 蒸馏到 4 步且把 CFG 折进模型、用分组 G-buffer 编码器 + 有状态微型解码器替换 Wan VAE
  • 实测：单张 H200 约 31 FPS，完整游戏循环 30 FPS；已与 SuperTuxKart 集成，带 Web UI、提示词切风格与键盘操控，仓库给推理代码与模型

为什么值得看：这是「生成式渲染」目前最接近引擎落地的形态：接口不用改架构（就是已有的 G-buffer），风格变成提示词而不是新模型。判断一个 AI 渲染方案能不能进项目，就看它敢不敢接结构化 G-buffer、以及能不能守住 30 FPS。

中文摘要：AlayaRenderer-Flash 是 AlayaRenderer 的实时版本，分工写得极清楚：游戏引擎继续模拟世界并导出 G-buffer（albedo、depth、metallic、normal、roughness），渲染器把这些缓冲渲染成 RGB 帧，风格由一句文本提示决定，速度按播放速率运行。工程上有三个关键手段：自回归渲染器维护压缩后的长、中、短三级 latent 历史，因此可以无限流式生成；从 50 步 teacher 蒸馏到 4 步，并把无分类器引导折进模型；用分组 G-buffer 编码器与有状态的微型解码器替换 Wan VAE。实测在单张 H200 上约 31 FPS，完整游戏循环保持 30 FPS；已与 SuperTuxKart 集成，带 Web UI、提示词切换风格与键盘操控，仓库包含推理代码与放出的模型。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：GitHub·AlayaLab（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-11-02

AlayaRenderer-Flash：以「游玩的速度」运行的生成式世界渲染器（Generative World Renderer at the Speed of Play）。

这是 AlayaRenderer 的实时版本。分工写在第一段里，非常直白：

The game engine keeps simulating the world and exports G-buffers (albedo, depth, metallic, normal, roughness). AlayaRenderer-Flash renders them into RGB frames in a style you set with a text prompt, at playback rate.

引擎继续跑仿真并导出 G-buffer（albedo、depth、metallic、normal、roughness），这个渲染器把 G-buffer 渲染成 RGB 帧，风格由一句文本提示决定，速度按播放速率跑。

五条工程指标

  • 可无限流式生成：自回归渲染器，维护压缩后的 长 / 中 / 短 三级 latent 历史；
  • 4 步出图：从 50 步 teacher 蒸馏，且把 classifier-free guidance 折进模型里；
  • 轻量编解码：用分组 G-buffer 编码器 + 有状态的微型解码器，替换掉 Wan VAE；
  • 实时：单张 H200 上约 31 FPS，完整游戏循环保持 30 FPS；
  • 能玩：与 SuperTuxKart 集成，带 Web UI、提示词切换风格、键盘操控。

仓库内容

推理代码、放出的 SuperTuxKart 模型，以及线上 demo（alaya-renderer-flash.alayalab.ai）背后的可玩版本。环境要求 Linux + NVIDIA 驱动 570+（CUDA 12.8）+ uv；uv sync 装环境，uv sync --extra demo 追加 OpenCV 用于实时 demo。也可以当库用：uv pip install "git+https://github.com/AlayaLab/AlayaRenderer-Flash.git"。

为什么这条重要

这是「AI 原生引擎」在渲染层最完整的一次工程落地：

  • 引擎没有退场，反而是仿真与状态的唯一负责人（G-buffer 就是契约）；
  • 生成模型退到「着色器/渲染管线」的位置，输入是结构化缓冲而不是文本或视频；
  • 风格从「模型权重」变成「一句提示词」，同一份 G-buffer 可以出不同美术风格；
  • 30 FPS 的完整游戏循环意味着它能接进真实玩法回路，而不是 demo 视频。

和 BoxWorld（引擎算状态、生成器渲染）比，这条更接近落地形态：接口是既有的 G-buffer，不需要引擎为模型改架构。

（正文为仓库 README 的整理与翻译。）

item.title: 流式交互视频终于有榜了：StreamEval 用 300 个「指令分批到达」的用例考 38 个模型，最难的是一路改还不崩 ｜ StreamEval: A Benchmark for Interactive Streaming Video Generation
item.description:
一句话：现有基准只测「生成质量」，不测「指令连续到达时还能不能守住身份与已改动内容」。

要点：

  • 痛点说得很准：现有基准（VBench、EvalCrafter 一路）是「给提示词→出一段视频→看画面」，而流式交互真正难的是指令连续到达、模型要在不中断生成的前提下响应新指令，同时守住人物身份、已有场景与之前所有有效修改
  • StreamEval 覆盖五类任务：数字人对话、虚拟人表演、世界生成、指令编辑、参考编辑；每类 60 个用例，时长分 15/30/60/120/300 秒五档，共 300 例、38 个模型（49 个模型-任务配置）
  • 十项指标分四维：任务执行、状态一致性、视觉保真度、声画协调，各指标 0–100 分；每个用例独立跑三次减少偶然；数据、代码、评分规则全开源并月度更新

为什么值得看：「交互世界模型」缺的从来不是又一个模型，而是一把能区分「会生成」和「会执行连续指令」的尺子。这条把评测重心从画面挪到状态一致性上，正好对应引擎侧最关心的「改动之后世界还是同一个世界吗」。

中文摘要：流式交互视频是今年最热的方向之一，但赛道连定义都没有共识，评测仍沿用「给提示词、出一段视频、看画质」的老框架——而实时交互真正难的是：用户指令是连续到达的，模型要在不中断生成的情况下及时响应新指令，同时保持人物身份、已有场景以及此前所有有效修改不变。StreamEval 因此提出一个面向流式交互视频的基准：五类任务（数字人对话、虚拟人表演、世界生成、指令编辑、参考编辑）各 60 个用例，时长覆盖 15 到 300 秒，共 300 例；十项指标归入任务执行、状态一致性、视觉保真与声画协调四个维度，每例独立跑三次，数据、代码与评分规则全部开源并月度更新。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-11-02

StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive
Streaming Video Generation Models

Abstract

We introduce StreamEval with four key features: First interactive streaming video generation benchmark.Fully open source. Benchmark data, evaluation code, protocols, and scoring rules are publicly available. Comprehensive coverage. Five tasks cover avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing, with 300 scripted cases lasting 15 to 300 seconds. Ten metrics assess task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. Monthly updates. We will evaluate new and updated models and publish leaderboard results monthly. Results from 38 models show that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai.

1 Introduction

As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important [72, 59]. Systems that generate video incrementally can accept new user inputs while a session is in progress [63, 5], supporting conversational avatars, controllable virtual worlds, and live video editing. Such settings require more than plausible individual frames or clips: generation and responsive control must remain aligned with incoming inputs as user requests and the surrounding context evolve over time.

Sustained interaction requires systems to execute new requests while preserving relevant prior content and state. A conversational avatar must respond in context without losing its identity or dialogue history; a generated world must accommodate new controls without disrupting unaffected scene content; and a video editor must apply, update, or remove edits while tracking an advancing source stream. Each request carries timing and scope requirements, defining when a change should occur, what it should modify, and what must remain intact. Evaluation must therefore assess both task execution and state consistency throughout a session alongside visual fidelity and audiovisual coordination.

Existing benchmarks examine complementary aspects of these requirements. VBench and EvalCrafter assess visual quality and temporal behavior, while T2V-CompBench examines compositional alignment [21, 41, 51]. WBench and WBench-Editing evaluate multi-turn control, successive edits, and content preservation within generated worlds [68, 36]. StreamAV-Bench assesses interactive updates and state retention in streaming video generation [39], and LongV2VBench examines editing quality over sustained source streams [59]. VideoFDB evaluates full-duplex conversational agents through their perception and generation of nonverbal audiovisual cues [44]. Its focus on conversational dynamics complements task-directed evaluation of request execution and state preservation. Building on these efforts, we bring avatar interaction, world generation, and real-time video editing into a unified benchmark with explicit, task-specific execution and preservation criteria.

We introduce StreamEval , spanning five tasks across these domains: digital-human dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing (figure1). The benchmark contains 300 scripted test cases, each representing a 15–300 s interactive session. A test case bundles the initial portrait, scene, or source video with a sequence of timed user requests and explicit criteria for what the output should change and preserve. For example, an editing case may change one object, update another while retaining the first edit, then remove an edit to restore the source. Inputs arrive incrementally, so the system must respond as the session unfolds. Ten task-specific metrics evaluate performance along four complementary dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. This framework structures evaluation across tasks while respecting differences in model input interfaces and metric applicability.

We evaluate 38 models on 300 test cases across five interactive streaming video tasks. Vidu S2 Avatar obtains the highest reported Dialogue score in digital-human dialogue. By Overall score, Vidu S2 Avatar leads avatar performance, MemFlow leads world generation, and Vidu S2 Editing leads both instruction and reference editing. Individual metrics reveal complementary strengths: LiveTalk obtains the highest Quality score in avatar performance, while JoyAI-Video-Edit obtains the highest Preservation score in instruction editing (section3.3). These results highlight distinct model strengths across tasks and interaction requirements. Looking ahead, we view real-time interactive video as an important challenge for bringing omni-modal models to diverse application settings.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    Unified interactive benchmark. Five streaming tasks and 300 scripted test cases specify timed multimodal inputs alongside explicit request-execution and state-preservation requirements.

  • •

    Multidimensional evaluation. Ten task-specific metrics assess task execution and state consistency alongside visual fidelity and audiovisual coordination under a shared session protocol.

  • •

    Cross-task system study. Evaluating 38 models across 300 test cases reveals limited instruction following in avatar performance and world generation, alongside low full-edit completion in reference editing.

    • 2 The StreamEval Benchmark

    2.1 Motivation

    Real-time interactive video is an important step toward omni-modal systems that continuously perceive, generate, and respond to evolving user needs. Evaluating this capability requires testing whether systems execute new requests while preserving relevant context and state. StreamEval addresses these requirements through five tasks spanning avatar interaction, world generation, and real-time video editing, with task-specific metrics defined in section3.2.

    Each test case specifies initialization, a timeline of incoming inputs, and expected outcomes. A scheduler releases inputs incrementally and advances editing sources on the session clock. Input events specify when controls arrive; scoring opportunities specify what the system must accomplish or retain.

    Avatar interaction.

    Digital-human dialogue requires contextually appropriate responses to user speech while maintaining persona and conversational history. Avatar performance requires rendering prescribed speech and requested visual actions, such as gaze shifts or hand gestures.

    World generation.

    World generation creates evolving scenes in response to successive controls over objects, actions, cameras, or spatial state, while preserving unaffected content and continuity.

    Real-time video editing.

    Instruction editing applies text-specified changes to an advancing video; reference editing uses images to specify the desired appearance. Both require modifying the intended target while preserving non-target content and source motion. Removal requests restore the contemporaneous source state.

    2.2 Benchmark Construction

    We pair online inputs with explicit state requirements (figure2). Qwen3.8-Max drafts session goals, timed controls, protected attributes, and expected outcomes. An authored oracle specifies what to establish, retain, cancel, or restore at each checkpoint. Media inputs are screened and revised against these requirements. All benchmark cases, including their timelines, oracles, and media, will be released together.

    Functional diversity and difficulty.

    Each task covers individual operations, combined requests, and recovery. Dialogue covers factual answers, cross-turn state, turn-taking, and interruption; performance covers speech, gaze, expression, pose, and gestures. World generation tests object and action control, state updates, and camera or spatial continuity. Editing tests target establishment, incremental updates, reference switching, scope preservation, and restoration. Repair, multi-target updates, and reappearance after occlusion add more demanding interactions within the same benchmark.

    Successive editing controls test whether established changes persist when new requests arrive. Cases include introducing a second target while retaining the first, updating selected attributes, switching references, and removing an edit to restore the advancing source.

    Avatar and world-generation inputs.

    GPT-Image-2 and Qwen-Image synthesize portraits and visual references; portraits depict original synthetic adults or stylized fictional characters. Qwen3.5-Omni generates expressive user and prescribed speech. Dialogue pairs these recordings with authored personas and verified facts, including recordings with background noise or reverberation. Paired text-dialogue derivatives replace audio turns with authored text while retaining identical source-family identities.

    Live editing sources.

    Editing tracks use continuous source videos comprising licensed real-world footage, animation, and benchmark-generated scenes. Third-party sources include Wikimedia Commons, NASA, and Blender Studio; per-asset licenses and attribution are supplied in the data release. Each source covers the session without looping, speed changes, or concatenation, so edits follow the advancing scene. Target regions are temporally grounded via Qwen3.8-Max at planned control timestamps.

    2.3 Data Statistics

    Release composition.

    Each task contains 60 test cases, balanced across 15, 30, 60, 120, and 300 seconds with 12 cases per duration. Across all five tracks, 300 test cases span 240 independent source families, with 60 text-dialogue derivatives reusing existing families. One pass through the 300 video-session cases represents 525 minutes of active streaming generation, excluding setup and response tails.

    Interaction load and diversity.

    The 300 test cases contain 1,347 planned online events, excluding initialization and continuous source frames. Inputs include speech, text, and visual references; each input can impose multiple execution and preservation requirements. Avatar designs span photorealistic, stylized 3D, anime, and clay or stop-motion appearances. Dialogue includes clean speech, background noise, and room reverberation, while editing covers indoor and outdoor scenes with single or multiple targets. Figure3 summarizes interaction statistics for 200 of these cases.

    Evaluation roster.

    The evaluation protocol specifies a roster of 300 test cases: 60 per task, with 12 at each duration tier and three independent runs per case and model. The results reported in this paper cover these 300 cases (section3.1). All five duration strata receive equal aggregation weight within each task, so longer sessions contribute equally to the final assessment rather than in proportion to their duration.

    2.4 Comparison with Existing Benchmarks

    Table1 positions StreamEval against existing video generation and interactive benchmarks across task coverage and evaluation horizons. Avatar-performance benchmarks assess rendered speakers, including visual quality and speech-motion synchronization, while Full-Duplex-Bench evaluates spoken dialogue without video output. VideoFDB additionally evaluates full-duplex conversational perception and audiovisual response generation [44]. Its naturally occurring nonverbal cues complement our authored speech-input dialogue and prescribed-performance tasks; our broader task coverage does not imply coverage of its user-video perception requirements. For video editing, WBench and WBench-Editing focus on world-model environments, while EditVerseBench covers instruction- and reference-conditioned editing of external videos [68, 36, 29]. WBench-Editing also reports a separate reference-conditioned comparison. Task interfaces and control timing jointly define the interaction protocol.

    StreamEval applies a balanced multi-horizon design across all five streaming tasks: 15, 30, 60, 120, and 300 seconds, with 60 test cases at each duration tier. Its 300-second editing cases represent a five-fold expansion over LongV2VBench (60 s), while its world-generation cases extend beyond StreamAV-Bench’s 180-second rollouts [59, 39]. Longer avatar sequences already appear in GenBench [20]; our contribution is balanced coverage across tasks and durations, with incrementally released multimodal controls and continuously advancing editing sources.

    We evaluate 38 models on 300 test cases across these tasks (section3.1). For context, WBench evaluates 20 models, WorldMark 10, and StreamAV-Bench 13 systems within their respective domains [68, 62, 39]. Our benchmark brings these application domains into a shared framework for assessing request execution and state preservation alongside content quality.

    2.5 Quality Verification

    Asset and consistency checks.

    Automated checks verify media decodability and duration bounds, file identity, and agreement among events, opportunities, and scoring requirements (figure2). Qwen3-ASR transcribes synthesized speech, requiring normalized word-error rates of at most 0.25 against authored transcripts. Qwen3.8-Max audits images for subject clarity and anatomical or rendering defects. Editing sources are checked for scene cuts, frozen spans, and unsuitable targets. Revised candidates must pass the same checks.

    Judge calibration.

    Targeted positive and negative probes evaluate automated production judges against acceptance criteria of at most 5% false positive rate, 10% false negative rate, and 10% unresolved decisions per class. Visual critique judges return structured defect categories, severity ratings, and supporting frame timestamps. Identity uses the lower rating from two judges given the same initialization portrait (or the system’s opening frame for a fixed avatar) and sampled output frames to guard against same-style identity substitutions.

    3 System Evaluation

    We evaluate how systems execute evolving requests, retain relevant state, and render the resulting video across the five tasks in section2. Each task and input setting has a defined metric profile and an Overall score.

    3.1 Evaluation Setup

    Evaluated models.

    We report 38 distinct models across 49 task configurations. A task configuration is a model evaluated on one task with its specified input route and any adapter components. A model evaluated on multiple tasks is counted once in the model total and separately for each task configuration. Avatar models include Vidu S2 Avatar [72], Tavus CVI Full, LiveAvatar FULL, Runway Characters, Vivix A1, AptAvatar, Avatar-Forever, AvatarForcing, AVTR-1, LiveTalk [5], MuseTalk [87], Quark Live Avatar, and the SoulX-FlashHead, SoulX-FlashTalk, and SoulX-LiveAct models. World generation covers AlayaWorld, HappyOyster 1.0 Adventure, HY-World 1.5 WorldPlay, LingBot-World 2.0, Matrix-Game 3.5, Causal Forcing, Context Forcing, Helios, Krea Realtime, LongLive 2.0, MemFlow, Reward Forcing, Rolling Forcing [40], Self-Forcing, ShotStream, Yume 1.5, and Zing-0.5. Reported editing models include Vidu S2 Editing, JoyAI-Video-Edit [59], EditaLive, Lucy 2.5 (Decart), SANA-Streaming, and XMax X2.0. The editing tables show configurations with Overall at least 5; this presentation subset was selected after evaluation. The model and configuration totals refer to the reported subset. LiveAvatar FULL and Tavus CVI Full use fixed, provider-supplied avatars because avatar customization is unavailable through their evaluated interfaces; Identity is rated against each system’s own opening frame and included in Overall, and their names appear in gray in table2.

    Evaluation tasks.

    The five tasks are digital-human dialogue (15 configurations), avatar performance (7), world generation (17: 12 text-conditioned and 5 image-conditioned), instruction editing (6), and reference editing (4). The evaluation covers 300 test cases (60 in each task) across five equally weighted duration strata from 15 to 300 s, with three repeats per test case and model. World generation includes text-controlled and image-conditioned inputs; the latter adds appearance conditioning.

    Evaluation metrics.

    We report ten metrics across four dimensions: task execution (Dialogue, Following, Edit Success), state consistency (Stability, Continuity, Preservation), visual fidelity (Quality, Identity, Reference), and audiovisual coordination (A–V Sync). Each task reports the equal-weight mean of its applicable metrics as Quality-Overall; avatar tasks additionally report a customization bonus and their sum as Overall.

    3.2 Metrics and Scoring

    3.2.1 Task-Specific Metrics

    Shared output measures.

    All five tasks assess output quality and stability under the expected state sequence, including authorized actions, edits, and restoration. Quality scores five-second clips from primary-judge defect lists: no defect, one minor defect, multiple minor defects, one severe defect, and multiple severe defects give ratings r∈{5,4,3,2,1}, respectively, with severe defects taking precedence and mapping to 25(r-1). Stability measures the duration covered by clips with no severe temporal defect, at most one minor temporal defect, and Quality rating at least 3. Because Stability is gated by Quality, the two metrics overlap and a high Stability score requires both temporal consistency and acceptable visual quality.

    Digital-human dialogue.

    Dialogue measures the percentage of planned turns satisfying answer, content, conversational, and timing requirements. Identity provides the initialization portrait (or the system’s own opening frame for a fixed avatar) and sampled clip frames to two judges, Qwen3.8-Max-0902 and Qwen3-VL-Plus, and takes the lower feature-derived rating while allowing authorized expression, pose, crop, and lighting changes. An explicitly different person or at least three clear feature changes gives rating 1; two clear changes give 2; one clear change or at least three slight changes gives 3; one or two slight changes give 4; no change gives 5. An unclear same-person judgment caps the rating at 3, and the final score is 25(r-1). A–V Sync measures the percentage of required speech events with lip-opening/audio-envelope correlation at least 0.3, evaluated at a pooled system offset whose 95% interval (2,000 session-bootstrap draws) lies within [-200,200] ms using 10-ms search steps over [-1000,1000] ms. Sparse source sampling (500 ms for dialogue, 250 ms for performance) limits its temporal resolution. Together with Quality and Stability, these metrics evaluate conversational execution, speaker appearance, and audiovisual delivery.

    Avatar performance.

    Following measures the percentage of control events in which the avatar executes the requested gaze, expression, pose, or gesture on the specified target. Prescribed speech supplies the verbal content. The task combines Following with Quality, Stability, Identity, and A–V Sync.

    World generation.

    Following measures the percentage of online controls that produce the requested scene operation on the specified target; a control passes when every frame in which the target is visible shows the requested outcome fully or partially. Continuity measures the fraction of generated duration meeting motion, camera, object-permanence, transition, and spatial-relation requirements. These two metrics join Quality and Stability in both the text-conditioned and the image-conditioned setting.

    Instruction editing.

    Following checks the requested operation and target, allowing a partial appearance match when no severe leakage occurs. Edit Success requires the complete edit to satisfy scope, active-state, deadline, persistence, and protected-content checks. Preservation assesses non-target content and current source motion, including restoration against the contemporaneous source. Together with Quality and Stability, this profile separates operation execution, full edit completion, source retention, and visual fidelity.

    Reference editing.

    Reference measures declared appearance attributes at checkpoints where the supplied image is active, whereas avatar Identity compares against the initialization portrait or, for fixed-avatar interfaces, the system’s opening frame. Edit Success checks the full editing contract, Preservation assesses protected source content and motion, and Quality and Stability complete the five-metric profile.

    Fixed rules convert structured visual observations into scores using each test case’s predefined deadline and verification window. Figure4 illustrates a recorded reference-editing session.

    3.2.2 Score Aggregation

    The ten content metrics use a 0–100 scale, with applicability fixed before inspecting outputs. Missing output and unsupported required operations receive zero, and all planned control opportunities remain in the denominator, including unfired triggers and controls beyond a provider’s session limit. Unresolved judgments define an interval by contributing 0 to the lower endpoint and 100 to the upper endpoint; tables report the lower endpoint when any required judgment is unresolved. Let s_c,r,m denote the run-level score for test case c, repeat r, and metric m, and let ℂ_d,m contain the applicable test cases in duration stratum d. We average the three repeats, then test cases within each stratum, and finally the five duration strata D:

    Sₘ=(1)/(|D|)∑_d∈D(1)/(|ℂ_d,m|)∑_c∈ℂ_d,m1/3∑ᵣ₌₁³s_c,r,m.

    		(1)

    Task-specific Overall.

    For task t and model k, let M_t,k contain its applicable metrics and S_t,k,m denote the metric aggregate from equation1. Quality-Overall is their equal-weight mean:

    QOverall_t,k=(1)/(|M_t,k|)∑_m∈M_t,kS_t,k,m.

    		(2)

    We abbreviate Quality-Overall as Q-Overall. Portrait-conditioned dialogue, performance, and both editing tasks average five metrics; fixed-avatar dialogue also averages five, because Identity is rated against the system’s own opening frame when its evaluated interface does not accept a custom portrait. World generation averages four metrics.

    Sweet-spot bonus for avatar customization.

    Avatar customization is an essential capability for digital-human dialogue and avatar performance, so these two tasks add a sweet-spot bonus to Q-Overall. Every system that supports a custom avatar receives +5; systems restricted to fixed, provider-supplied avatars receive 0. The tables report Q-Overall, the bonus (Custom.), and their sum as Overall, which orders the avatar tasks. All other tasks report Overall = Q-Overall. Thus,

    Overall_t,k=QOverall_t,k+B_t,k, B_t,k=\begincases5,&avatar task with custom-avatar support, 0,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(3)

    Q-Overall remains on a 0–100 scale; the avatar ranking score can reach 105. The bonus describes interface capability and does not alter the underlying metric scores.

    3.3 Experimental Results

    Tables2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 report model performance across the five tasks in alphabetical order. The website shows the same scores sorted by descending Overall within each task.

    3.3.1 Digital-Human Dialogue

    Among custom-avatar models, Vidu S2 Avatar achieves the highest Overall score (93.98; 88.98 Q-Overall plus the customization bonus) and leads in Quality (96.78), Dialogue (75.29), and Identity (90.12), followed by AVTR-1 at 84.14 Overall (79.14 Q-Overall), 82.97 Quality, and 88.54 Identity (table2). In the fixed-avatar setting, where Identity is rated against each system’s own opening frame, Tavus CVI Full reaches 86.65 Q-Overall and 89.89 Identity compared with 65.07 and 87.70 for LiveAvatar FULL; neither supports a custom avatar, so both receive no bonus and their Overall equals Q-Overall. Across individual shared dimensions, Tavus CVI Full records the highest A–V Sync (94.44 vs. 84.87 for Vidu S2 Avatar) and the second-highest Dialogue (73.91, behind Vidu S2 Avatar at 75.29 and ahead of 61.37 for LiveAvatar FULL), while LiveAvatar FULL reaches 100.00 in Stability alongside 0.00 in A–V Sync.

    Results among models evaluated with the shared dialogue pipeline further show that strong visual appearance and temporal stability do not automatically accompany high synchronization or conversational scores. MuseTalk 1.5 [87] attains 95.34 in Quality, 97.11 in Stability, and 88.44 in Identity, yet records 38.09 in A–V Sync and 54.34 in Dialogue (79.66 Overall). Conversely, AptAvatar 14B reaches 70.32 in A–V Sync and 94.74 in Stability, but scores 35.98 in Dialogue and 68.03 in Quality (75.01 Overall), whereas SoulX-FlashTalk 14B records 68.90 Quality, 66.27 A–V Sync, and 50.57 Dialogue to reach 77.90 Overall.

一句话：现有基准只测「生成质量」，不测「指令连续到达时还能不能守住身份与已改动内容」。

要点：

  • 痛点说得很准：现有基准（VBench、EvalCrafter 一路）是「给提示词→出一段视频→看画面」，而流式交互真正难的是指令连续到达、模型要在不中断生成的前提下响应新指令，同时守住人物身份、已有场景与之前所有有效修改
  • StreamEval 覆盖五类任务：数字人对话、虚拟人表演、世界生成、指令编辑、参考编辑；每类 60 个用例，时长分 15/30/60/120/300 秒五档，共 300 例、38 个模型（49 个模型-任务配置）
  • 十项指标分四维：任务执行、状态一致性、视觉保真度、声画协调，各指标 0–100 分；每个用例独立跑三次减少偶然；数据、代码、评分规则全开源并月度更新

为什么值得看：「交互世界模型」缺的从来不是又一个模型，而是一把能区分「会生成」和「会执行连续指令」的尺子。这条把评测重心从画面挪到状态一致性上，正好对应引擎侧最关心的「改动之后世界还是同一个世界吗」。

中文摘要：流式交互视频是今年最热的方向之一，但赛道连定义都没有共识，评测仍沿用「给提示词、出一段视频、看画质」的老框架——而实时交互真正难的是：用户指令是连续到达的，模型要在不中断生成的情况下及时响应新指令，同时保持人物身份、已有场景以及此前所有有效修改不变。StreamEval 因此提出一个面向流式交互视频的基准：五类任务（数字人对话、虚拟人表演、世界生成、指令编辑、参考编辑）各 60 个用例，时长覆盖 15 到 300 秒，共 300 例；十项指标归入任务执行、状态一致性、视觉保真与声画协调四个维度，每例独立跑三次，数据、代码与评分规则全部开源并月度更新。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-11-02

StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive
Streaming Video Generation Models

Abstract

We introduce StreamEval with four key features: First interactive streaming video generation benchmark.Fully open source. Benchmark data, evaluation code, protocols, and scoring rules are publicly available. Comprehensive coverage. Five tasks cover avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing, with 300 scripted cases lasting 15 to 300 seconds. Ten metrics assess task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. Monthly updates. We will evaluate new and updated models and publish leaderboard results monthly. Results from 38 models show that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai.

1 Introduction

As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important [72, 59]. Systems that generate video incrementally can accept new user inputs while a session is in progress [63, 5], supporting conversational avatars, controllable virtual worlds, and live video editing. Such settings require more than plausible individual frames or clips: generation and responsive control must remain aligned with incoming inputs as user requests and the surrounding context evolve over time.

Sustained interaction requires systems to execute new requests while preserving relevant prior content and state. A conversational avatar must respond in context without losing its identity or dialogue history; a generated world must accommodate new controls without disrupting unaffected scene content; and a video editor must apply, update, or remove edits while tracking an advancing source stream. Each request carries timing and scope requirements, defining when a change should occur, what it should modify, and what must remain intact. Evaluation must therefore assess both task execution and state consistency throughout a session alongside visual fidelity and audiovisual coordination.

Existing benchmarks examine complementary aspects of these requirements. VBench and EvalCrafter assess visual quality and temporal behavior, while T2V-CompBench examines compositional alignment [21, 41, 51]. WBench and WBench-Editing evaluate multi-turn control, successive edits, and content preservation within generated worlds [68, 36]. StreamAV-Bench assesses interactive updates and state retention in streaming video generation [39], and LongV2VBench examines editing quality over sustained source streams [59]. VideoFDB evaluates full-duplex conversational agents through their perception and generation of nonverbal audiovisual cues [44]. Its focus on conversational dynamics complements task-directed evaluation of request execution and state preservation. Building on these efforts, we bring avatar interaction, world generation, and real-time video editing into a unified benchmark with explicit, task-specific execution and preservation criteria.

We introduce StreamEval , spanning five tasks across these domains: digital-human dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing (figure1). The benchmark contains 300 scripted test cases, each representing a 15–300 s interactive session. A test case bundles the initial portrait, scene, or source video with a sequence of timed user requests and explicit criteria for what the output should change and preserve. For example, an editing case may change one object, update another while retaining the first edit, then remove an edit to restore the source. Inputs arrive incrementally, so the system must respond as the session unfolds. Ten task-specific metrics evaluate performance along four complementary dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. This framework structures evaluation across tasks while respecting differences in model input interfaces and metric applicability.

We evaluate 38 models on 300 test cases across five interactive streaming video tasks. Vidu S2 Avatar obtains the highest reported Dialogue score in digital-human dialogue. By Overall score, Vidu S2 Avatar leads avatar performance, MemFlow leads world generation, and Vidu S2 Editing leads both instruction and reference editing. Individual metrics reveal complementary strengths: LiveTalk obtains the highest Quality score in avatar performance, while JoyAI-Video-Edit obtains the highest Preservation score in instruction editing (section3.3). These results highlight distinct model strengths across tasks and interaction requirements. Looking ahead, we view real-time interactive video as an important challenge for bringing omni-modal models to diverse application settings.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    Unified interactive benchmark. Five streaming tasks and 300 scripted test cases specify timed multimodal inputs alongside explicit request-execution and state-preservation requirements.

  • •

    Multidimensional evaluation. Ten task-specific metrics assess task execution and state consistency alongside visual fidelity and audiovisual coordination under a shared session protocol.

  • •

    Cross-task system study. Evaluating 38 models across 300 test cases reveals limited instruction following in avatar performance and world generation, alongside low full-edit completion in reference editing.

    • 2 The StreamEval Benchmark

    2.1 Motivation

    Real-time interactive video is an important step toward omni-modal systems that continuously perceive, generate, and respond to evolving user needs. Evaluating this capability requires testing whether systems execute new requests while preserving relevant context and state. StreamEval addresses these requirements through five tasks spanning avatar interaction, world generation, and real-time video editing, with task-specific metrics defined in section3.2.

    Each test case specifies initialization, a timeline of incoming inputs, and expected outcomes. A scheduler releases inputs incrementally and advances editing sources on the session clock. Input events specify when controls arrive; scoring opportunities specify what the system must accomplish or retain.

    Avatar interaction.

    Digital-human dialogue requires contextually appropriate responses to user speech while maintaining persona and conversational history. Avatar performance requires rendering prescribed speech and requested visual actions, such as gaze shifts or hand gestures.

    World generation.

    World generation creates evolving scenes in response to successive controls over objects, actions, cameras, or spatial state, while preserving unaffected content and continuity.

    Real-time video editing.

    Instruction editing applies text-specified changes to an advancing video; reference editing uses images to specify the desired appearance. Both require modifying the intended target while preserving non-target content and source motion. Removal requests restore the contemporaneous source state.

    2.2 Benchmark Construction

    We pair online inputs with explicit state requirements (figure2). Qwen3.8-Max drafts session goals, timed controls, protected attributes, and expected outcomes. An authored oracle specifies what to establish, retain, cancel, or restore at each checkpoint. Media inputs are screened and revised against these requirements. All benchmark cases, including their timelines, oracles, and media, will be released together.

    Functional diversity and difficulty.

    Each task covers individual operations, combined requests, and recovery. Dialogue covers factual answers, cross-turn state, turn-taking, and interruption; performance covers speech, gaze, expression, pose, and gestures. World generation tests object and action control, state updates, and camera or spatial continuity. Editing tests target establishment, incremental updates, reference switching, scope preservation, and restoration. Repair, multi-target updates, and reappearance after occlusion add more demanding interactions within the same benchmark.

    Successive editing controls test whether established changes persist when new requests arrive. Cases include introducing a second target while retaining the first, updating selected attributes, switching references, and removing an edit to restore the advancing source.

    Avatar and world-generation inputs.

    GPT-Image-2 and Qwen-Image synthesize portraits and visual references; portraits depict original synthetic adults or stylized fictional characters. Qwen3.5-Omni generates expressive user and prescribed speech. Dialogue pairs these recordings with authored personas and verified facts, including recordings with background noise or reverberation. Paired text-dialogue derivatives replace audio turns with authored text while retaining identical source-family identities.

    Live editing sources.

    Editing tracks use continuous source videos comprising licensed real-world footage, animation, and benchmark-generated scenes. Third-party sources include Wikimedia Commons, NASA, and Blender Studio; per-asset licenses and attribution are supplied in the data release. Each source covers the session without looping, speed changes, or concatenation, so edits follow the advancing scene. Target regions are temporally grounded via Qwen3.8-Max at planned control timestamps.

    2.3 Data Statistics

    Release composition.

    Each task contains 60 test cases, balanced across 15, 30, 60, 120, and 300 seconds with 12 cases per duration. Across all five tracks, 300 test cases span 240 independent source families, with 60 text-dialogue derivatives reusing existing families. One pass through the 300 video-session cases represents 525 minutes of active streaming generation, excluding setup and response tails.

    Interaction load and diversity.

    The 300 test cases contain 1,347 planned online events, excluding initialization and continuous source frames. Inputs include speech, text, and visual references; each input can impose multiple execution and preservation requirements. Avatar designs span photorealistic, stylized 3D, anime, and clay or stop-motion appearances. Dialogue includes clean speech, background noise, and room reverberation, while editing covers indoor and outdoor scenes with single or multiple targets. Figure3 summarizes interaction statistics for 200 of these cases.

    Evaluation roster.

    The evaluation protocol specifies a roster of 300 test cases: 60 per task, with 12 at each duration tier and three independent runs per case and model. The results reported in this paper cover these 300 cases (section3.1). All five duration strata receive equal aggregation weight within each task, so longer sessions contribute equally to the final assessment rather than in proportion to their duration.

    2.4 Comparison with Existing Benchmarks

    Table1 positions StreamEval against existing video generation and interactive benchmarks across task coverage and evaluation horizons. Avatar-performance benchmarks assess rendered speakers, including visual quality and speech-motion synchronization, while Full-Duplex-Bench evaluates spoken dialogue without video output. VideoFDB additionally evaluates full-duplex conversational perception and audiovisual response generation [44]. Its naturally occurring nonverbal cues complement our authored speech-input dialogue and prescribed-performance tasks; our broader task coverage does not imply coverage of its user-video perception requirements. For video editing, WBench and WBench-Editing focus on world-model environments, while EditVerseBench covers instruction- and reference-conditioned editing of external videos [68, 36, 29]. WBench-Editing also reports a separate reference-conditioned comparison. Task interfaces and control timing jointly define the interaction protocol.

    StreamEval applies a balanced multi-horizon design across all five streaming tasks: 15, 30, 60, 120, and 300 seconds, with 60 test cases at each duration tier. Its 300-second editing cases represent a five-fold expansion over LongV2VBench (60 s), while its world-generation cases extend beyond StreamAV-Bench’s 180-second rollouts [59, 39]. Longer avatar sequences already appear in GenBench [20]; our contribution is balanced coverage across tasks and durations, with incrementally released multimodal controls and continuously advancing editing sources.

    We evaluate 38 models on 300 test cases across these tasks (section3.1). For context, WBench evaluates 20 models, WorldMark 10, and StreamAV-Bench 13 systems within their respective domains [68, 62, 39]. Our benchmark brings these application domains into a shared framework for assessing request execution and state preservation alongside content quality.

    2.5 Quality Verification

    Asset and consistency checks.

    Automated checks verify media decodability and duration bounds, file identity, and agreement among events, opportunities, and scoring requirements (figure2). Qwen3-ASR transcribes synthesized speech, requiring normalized word-error rates of at most 0.25 against authored transcripts. Qwen3.8-Max audits images for subject clarity and anatomical or rendering defects. Editing sources are checked for scene cuts, frozen spans, and unsuitable targets. Revised candidates must pass the same checks.

    Judge calibration.

    Targeted positive and negative probes evaluate automated production judges against acceptance criteria of at most 5% false positive rate, 10% false negative rate, and 10% unresolved decisions per class. Visual critique judges return structured defect categories, severity ratings, and supporting frame timestamps. Identity uses the lower rating from two judges given the same initialization portrait (or the system’s opening frame for a fixed avatar) and sampled output frames to guard against same-style identity substitutions.

    3 System Evaluation

A model evaluated on multiple tasks is counted once in the model total and separately for each task configuration. World generation covers AlayaWorld, HappyOyster 1.0 Adventure, HY-World 1.5 WorldPlay, LingBot-World 2.0, Matrix-Game 3.5, Causal Forcing, Context Forcing, Helios, Krea Realtime, LongLive 2.0, MemFlow, Reward Forcing, Rolling Forcing [40], Self-Forcing, ShotStream, Yume 1.5, and Zing-0.5. Reported editing models include Vidu S2 Editing, JoyAI-Video-Edit [59], EditaLive, Lucy 2.5 (Decart), SANA-Streaming, and XMax X2.0. The editing tables show configurations with Overall at least 5; this presentation subset was selected after evaluation. The model and configuration totals refer to the reported subset.     Tables2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 report model performance across the five tasks in alphabetical order. The website shows the same scores sorted by descending Overall within each task.

    3.3.1 Digital-Human Dialogue

    Among custom-avatar models, Vidu S2 Avatar achieves the highest Overall score (93.98; 88.98 Q-Overall plus the customization bonus) and leads in Quality (96.78), Dialogue (75.29), and Identity (90.12), followed by AVTR-1 at 84.14 Overall (79.14 Q-Overall), 82.97 Quality, and 88.54 Identity (table2). In the fixed-avatar setting, where Identity is rated against each system’s own opening frame, Tavus CVI Full reaches 86.65 Q-Overall and 89.89 Identity compared with 65.07 and 87.70 for LiveAvatar FULL; neither supports a custom avatar, so both receive no bonus and their Overall equals Q-Overall. Across individual shared dimensions, Tavus CVI Full records the highest A–V Sync (94.44 vs. 84.87 for Vidu S2 Avatar) and the second-highest Dialogue (73.91, behind Vidu S2 Avatar at 75.29 and ahead of 61.37 for LiveAvatar FULL), while LiveAvatar FULL reaches 100.00 in Stability alongside 0.00 in A–V Sync.

    Results among models evaluated with the shared dialogue pipeline further show that strong visual appearance and temporal stability do not automatically accompany high synchronization or conversational scores. MuseTalk 1.5 [87] attains 95.34 in Quality, 97.11 in Stability, and 88.44 in Identity, yet records 38.09 in A–V Sync and 54.34 in Dialogue (79.66 Overall). Conversely, AptAvatar 14B reaches 70.32 in A–V Sync and 94.74 in Stability, but scores 35.98 in Dialogue and 68.03 in Quality (75.01 Overall), whereas SoulX-FlashTalk 14B records 68.90 Quality, 66.27 A–V Sync, and 50.57 Dialogue to reach 77.90 Overall.

item.title: 世界模型的回报算错了，错在「事件」而不是像素：把想象的转移换成真实的，误差会掉多少一眼就看出来 ｜ Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong
item.description:
一句话：画面忠实但回报算错是常态；作者做「转移级」诊断，定位误差集中在少数事件转移上。

要点：

  • 现象：世界模型被用于规划时，planner 按模型想象的回报给动作排序，但这些模型主要还是按「渲染得像不像」被评价——而一段视觉上忠实的 rollout 完全可能给出错误回报
  • 方法是一个「转移级」诊断：把想象中的转移替换成真实转移，测量回报误差的下降幅度，并与预算匹配的随机对照比较，从而把误差归因到具体的时间步
  • 结论有两条，第一条是「事件转移」——少数关键事件（物体交互、状态切换）承担了大部分回报误差；这解释了为什么画面指标看不出来的问题会在规划上翻车

为什么值得看：引擎侧接世界模型做 AI 决策时，最危险的就是「画面对了、因果错了」。这条给的是一个可执行的诊断协议：逐转移替换 + 随机对照，不需要重训模型就能定位「回报是在哪一步算错的」。

中文摘要：世界模型越来越多被用于规划：planner 按模型想象出的回报给候选动作排序。但这些模型主要仍按「渲染得像不像」被评价，而一段视觉上忠实的 rollout 依然可能给出错误的回报。为定位这种错配出现在哪里，作者提出一种「转移级」诊断：把想象中的转移替换成真实转移，测量回报误差的下降量，并与预算匹配的随机对照相比；这样可以把误差归因到具体时间步。分析得到两条发现，第一条是「事件转移」——少数关键事件（如物体交互与状态切换）承担了回报误差的主要部分，而像素级指标对此几乎不敏感。对要用世界模型做决策的系统，这提供了一套不需要重训就能定位回报错误的协议。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-11-02

Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong

Abstract

World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model–collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4×10⁻⁷), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.

1 Introduction

World models let an agent imagine the consequences of an action before taking it [18]. A planner rolls candidate action sequences forward inside the model and acts on the ordering of their imagined returns [11, 20, 48, 23, 22, 2, 36]. Released pixel world models support this pipeline in Atari, continuous control, and manipulation [12, 60, 52], and their progress is mainly measured by how faithfully they render the future [59, 65, 53].

Rendering quality, however, is only loosely tied to what a planner needs. A return often hinges on a few transitions that carry a reward or end an episode, so a model can render a rollout well yet misprice it by missing a single paddle contact. Model-level studies expose this mismatch: rankings by visual quality can disagree with rankings by task success [33, 64], and whole-model oracle substitutions find that average prediction accuracy does not consistently explain planning performance [41, 49, 7]. Yet neither these analyses nor compounding-error bounds [26] reveal where that error occurs: is it spread across all sixty steps of a rollout, or concentrated in only a few? We therefore ask:

Where inside an imagined rollout does the error that changes a planner’s decision occur?

To answer this question, we introduce a transition-level substitution diagnostic (Fig. 1). Each imagined rollout is paired with a real rollout that starts from the same context and follows the same recorded actions, so the two differ only in who drew the frames. A frozen, memoryless detector, trained once per game, reads reward and termination from each pair of consecutive frames; replacing one imagined pair with the real one therefore changes the return only at that step. We patch the pairs at true events, the same number of random pairs, all non-event pairs, or every pair. These four patches isolate the targeting effect, its budget-matched control, the error away from events, and an all-real reference.

Our analysis yields two findings. First, return error concentrates at events that do not look wrong. In Fig. 1D, restoring three transitions around a Seaquest reward removes almost all return error; three random ones remove little. Across 44 reliable Atari model–collection pairs, event patches beat random patches in 39 by a median of +44 points, and the advantage appears within a few patches (Fig. 2). Event frames are rendered as well as others (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error; the same pattern holds on eighteen games added after our predictions were recorded. Second, the remaining error is structured rather than merely mistimed. Complementary patches separate errors at true events from errors elsewhere, and timing-tolerant recall shows that temporal offset explains little of the events our deterministic models miss. This structure also predicts where a diffusion model helps; event patches improve plan ranking and carry over to control tasks with rare reward events.

We summarise our contributions as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a per-transition substitution diagnostic with a budget-matched random control. It treats the world model as a black box, and we apply it to three released model families on all 26 Atari-100k games.

  • •

    We show, for the first time on released pixel world models, that return error concentrates at reward and termination transitions, also under each model’s own reward head and without the score display, and that a complementary patch separates errors at true events from other errors.

  • •

    We show that a temporal offset explains little of the events missed by deterministic models, predict all four repair outcomes with a rule recorded in advance, and show that event patches improve plan ranking in every counted pair and carry over to control tasks with rare reward events.

    • 2 Related Work

    Pixel world models support prediction and control in games [40, 10, 29, 21, 46, 66, 36, 37, 2, 12] and interactive video simulators [62, 6, 54, 60]. Yet visual fidelity can diverge from physical correctness [38] and task success [33, 64, 58]; the same disconnect appears for training likelihood [31, 13, 16], synthetic training data [1], and token pruning [57]. Concurrent work weights error by decision-relevant state dimensions [56], while DIAMOND shows that visual details matter [2]. We instead locate where decision-relevant error occurs inside a rollout.

    Oracle substitution localises such failures. Cloning Deterministic Worlds [61] substitutes true states for learned representations, while whole-model oracle interventions relate accuracy to planning [41, 49, 7]; a concurrent diagnostic uses a kinematic null [47]. Closest to ours, counterfactual debugging [32] assigns Shapley credit over time steps to a policy’s sim-to-real gap under injected faults, and agent explanations identify steps that decide a return [17, 8, 3]. We instead operate directly on released world-model rollouts, replacing individual transition pairs under a budget-matched random control. This brings perturbation-based attribution [63, 14, 44, 25], used and tested on Atari agents [15, 4], from pixels to time steps.

    Other work improves prediction with multi-step training [50, 55], goal-aware objectives [39], keyframe targets [27, 43], region- and event-aware objectives [34, 42], causal rollout structure [67], and architecture-level probing [28]. Conditional-mean effects are also studied in video prediction [35] and perception and driving models [45]. We test which explanation accounts for missed events using event survival, a diffusion model, and the same network trained deterministically.

    3 Diagnostic Setup

    The diagnostic needs only rendered frames, so it applies to released checkpoints without access to their internals.

    Return from a Predicted Trajectory.

    A probe is a real context with fixed actions a_1:H (Fig. 1A); from it, a model produces imagined observations ô_1:H. A frozen detector, shared by all world models of a game, reads each transition pair and its action as a reward sign and a termination flag, (r̂ₜ,d̂ₜ)=D(ôₜ,ôₜ₊₁,aₜ) for t

    Ĝ=∑ₜ₌₁^Hγᵗ⁻¹sgn(r̂ₜ)∏_j

    		(1)

    where G is computed in the same way from r and d, and 𝔼 averages over probes. Atari uses H=60 and γ=0.99.

    Substitutions and Their Controls.

    For channel c (observation o, reward r or termination d) and a binary mask m, let Ĝ^c,m be the return after substituting the selected real information (Fig. 1). Observation patches replace both frames of the selected transition before detection, so no pair mixes real and generated frames; unselected pairs keep their predictions. Reward and termination interventions replace r̂ or d̂. We report the fractional reduction in mean absolute return error:

    R(c,m)=1-(𝔼[|Ĝ^c,m-G|])/(𝔼[|Ĝ-G|]).

    		(2)

    The all-frame value R(o,1) measures performance when the detector sees only real transition pairs.

    The event mask starts from nonzero real reward or termination and is dilated by one step, i.e., the transitions just before and after are also selected, to cover delays in the visual markers. We report its realised coverage q=\penalty𝔼[H⁻¹∑ₜmₜ^\rmev], which includes dilation. The random mask selects the same number of steps in each rollout. The targeting advantage is

    L=R(o,m^\rmev)-R(o,m^\rmrnd).

    		(3)

    The complementary mask m̄^\rmev measures errors away from the selected events, and its contrast with the event patch classifies the failure pattern of each model.

    4 Localising the Return Error

    We localise the return error with one frozen, memoryless detector per game, shared by every world model of that game. A random patch also hits true events, and more of them as coverage grows, so the lift of Eq. (3) credits the event patch only with what it adds beyond chance.

    Figure 2 widens the event neighbourhood step by step and plots the lift against the resulting coverage. In 8 of 9 sweeps over three games and three released families, the event curve stays well above the random curve. For DIAMOND on Freeway, patching 2.8 of sixty steps removes 69% of the error, against -4% for random patches and 86% when every frame is real; on Pong, 2.1 steps remove 43% against 5%. The sweep also exposes a timing effect: without dilation the Freeway event patch is negative, consistent with the reward digit appearing after the transition that earns it, so we treat the neighbourhood as part of the measurement.

    The sweep also shows why the random control is needed. For DIAMOND and Simulus on Seaquest, both patches remove more error as coverage grows while the lift stays flat, so the event-patch reduction alone would overstate the targeting effect. Table 1 reports every game at a one-step neighbourhood, and Fig. 3 shows events beyond Atari.

    5 Missing Events and a Model-Class Repair

    Localisation shows where the return error lies, not why. We ask why imagined events are missed and whether another model class draws them.

    5.1 Absent or Mistimed Events

    A detector can miss an event in imagined frames for two reasons: the model draws it at a neighbouring step, or it does not draw it in a form the detector reads. The two predict different curves. If events are only mistimed, recall should rise with the alignment tolerance faster than for a displaced-prediction null; if they are not drawn readably, recall should stay low at every tolerance.

    5.2 A Rule Recorded Before the Outcomes

    If events are not drawn readably, a model that draws them should reduce the return error, most where the baseline misses most events. As a repair, we replace our deterministic MSE predictor with a diffusion model trained on the same data [24, 30, 2], which samples each next observation instead of regressing it (“sampling” in figures and tables). A sampled future can differ from the realised one, so we evaluate event recall, return error, and plan ranking.

    Before observing the remaining outcomes, we pre-specified this rule: a baseline event recall at τ=0 below 0.50 predicts a return-error reduction larger than the declared floor of that game, and a recall at or above 0.50 predicts no such reduction. The threshold is a heuristic for the headroom left by missing events; floors and failure conditions were fixed at the same stage. Freeway had already been scored, so the prospective score covers Pong and the three unrun sampling arms. The MSE baseline gets more training, 30k updates against 8k, because at 8k updates it detects no return on Freeway and Pong; data, sequence length, batch size, learning rate, and seeds match (supplement).

    6 Experiments

    In this section, we carry out experiments to address the following questions: Q1: Is the return error concentrated at event transitions (Sec. 6.2)? Q2: Are missed events absent or only mistimed (Sec. 6.3)? Q3: Does a diffusion model repair them as recorded (Sec. 6.4)? Q4: Do the same transitions drive plan selection (Sec. 6.5)?

    6.1 Experimental Setup

    We study 26 Atari games [5] with 64×64 observations and frameskip four, using Atari-100k [29] model checkpoints [2, 36, 12]. Across three released families and three locally trained random-policy Breakout models, 44 pairs clear reliability checks. Transfer evaluation adds 9 rows across 6 DeepMind Control tasks [51] and released iVideoGPT on robosuite [68, 60, 52].

    Atari attribution uses 400 probes, each paired with a real trajectory under the same actions. Each frozen detector must reach a reward-event F1 of 0.90 on an independent collection with environment seeds disjoint from its training data. Terminations are read but not gated; replacing them removes a median 0.7% of the return error. The real reward at the last step stays in the all-real residual (median 1.5% of the error; supplement). Figure 7 adds matched-action RSSM [20] and Transformer predictions on MiniGrid [9] and Crafter [19].

    6.2 A1: Return Error Concentrates at Events

    Main Results. As shown in Table 1, the event patch has positive lift in 39 of 44 counted pairs (sign test p=1.4×10⁻⁷), with a median of +44 points (probe-bootstrap 95% intervals: 38 above zero, 2 spanning it, 4 below). Each released family and every counted game except MsPacman has a positive median lift (per-game sign test, p=5.2×10⁻⁴); three sampling seeds change lift by a median of 2.0 points, and other discounts and horizons keep 39–41 pairs positive (supplement). As a patch changes only the selected transitions, event transitions cause most of the return error.

    Robustness to the Reward Reader. To rule out our detector, we use each model’s reward head: all 25 pairs whose head reads real futures reliably stay positive (median +46; rank correlation 0.85 with our detector), as do 6 pairs from games it cannot read. Hiding the score display keeps all 6 Pong and Freeway pairs positive (median +64; supplement).

    Comparison with Pixel Error. One may expect the error to sit in poorly rendered frames. Yet event frames are rendered as well as other frames (median ratio 0.85), and as shown in Table 2, the transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error are events only about as often as random picks, so patching them removes less than random patches. Pixel metrics thus cannot locate the return error.

    Effect of Coverage. Random patches hit more events as q grows, so a lift that only reflected sparse events would vanish. Yet the median lift is +40 above q=12% (+59 below 6%), and all Krull pairs stay positive at q=58.5%.

    Failure Patterns. With R_\rmev=R(o,m^\rmev) and the complementary patch’s R_\rmnon=R(o,m̄^\rmev), a pair is event-dominated if R_\rmev-R_\rmnon>0.20, non-event-dominated if it is below -0.20, and unclassified otherwise; the counts are 33, 5 and 6. Simulus on Freeway is event-dominated: event patches remove 72% and the complement -16%. DIAMOND on Boxing is the opposite: it imagines a return of 6.67 against a true 2.31, and event patches remove 12% and the complement 72%, so under our detector its excess return lies away from true scoring events. Under its own reward model, it is event-dominated (supplement). Most pairs thus fail by missing true events.

    6.3 A2: Missed Events Persist Under Tolerance

    We next ask whether missed events are merely mistimed (Sec. 5.1). To investigate this, we compare reward-event recall at alignment tolerance τ with a circularly displaced copy of the predictions, which keeps their event rate. If events were only mistimed, widening τ would recover most of them. As shown in Figs. 4 and 5, it recovers few: on Freeway, the MSE baseline recovers 0.091 of the events at τ=0 and 0.153 at τ=8, against 0.028 for the null, and across the five games at least 76% of its recall deficit remains at τ=8. Most missed events are thus absent rather than mistimed. DIAMOND on Freeway recovers more (0.767 to 0.932), and the diffusion model already reaches 0.943 at τ=0.

    6.4 A3: A Diffusion Model Repairs as Predicted

    If missing events cause the return error, a model that draws them should reduce it. As shown in Table 3, all four comparisons clear their floors, and the pre-specified rule scores 4/4, including 3/3 on the games whose detector passes the attribution gate. Three sampling seeds on Freeway and Pong give error ranges of 0.0356 and 0.0278, both below ΔE.

    Ablation on Sampling. A natural question is whether the gain comes from sampling. To isolate it, we train the same diffusion network with a deterministic squared-error objective (same data, 8k updates and seeds). It still has lower error than our MSE baseline on all five games and keeps Freeway’s events (recall 0.95 against 0.94); its seed-mean error is lower than with sampling on Freeway (0.096 against 0.171) and within the larger seed span on the other four, while sampling recalls more events on Pong (0.80 against 0.69; supplement). The repair thus comes from the diffusion network, not from sampling or the training loss.

    6.5 A4: Event Transitions Drive Plan Selection

    Finally, if events decide the imagined return, restoring them should also improve plan choice beyond a matched random patch. To test this, we rank eight plans from each of 150 emulator states, as a sampling-based planner does [11, 20], and score pairwise accuracy and normalised top-1 regret; 7 of the twelve pairs, including the diffusion model, pass the reliability rules (supplement), and Fig. 7 shows one. The event patch improves pairwise accuracy in all 7 pairs, whereas a random patch changes it by a median of +0.019, and median top-1 regret falls from 0.565 to 0.141. Under pre-specified rules, 15 further games add 8 pairs from Freeway, CrazyClimber and Gopher, whose detectors also pass on plan states, and the event patch improves all 8 of them (median +0.156, random +0.012; supplement). On Pong, the diffusion model raises pairwise accuracy from 0.5000 to 0.6110 (random-weighted control 0.5007). The transitions carrying the return error thus also decide plan selection.

    7 Cross-Task Transfer and Discussion

    Beyond Atari, we apply the diagnostic to six DeepMind Control tasks and robosuite, and compare matched-action rollouts on MiniGrid and Crafter (Fig. 7). On the control tasks of Fig. 3, the three comparisons whose detector passes yield +54/+54 points of lift on sparse cartpole across two architectures and +8 on ball-in-cup (supplement).

    Concurrent work finds ball disappearance and invalid ball–paddle interactions in five frozen Pong world models [34]; we locate the return error across 26 games.

    8 Conclusion

    In this paper, we introduce a per-transition substitution diagnostic that locates where the imagined return of a world model goes wrong. In 39 of 44 reliably measured model–collection pairs on Atari-100k, the return error concentrates at reward and termination transitions that pixel metrics do not single out: world models get the return wrong at events, in frames that look no worse than the rest. A rule recorded in advance predicts where a diffusion model class helps, and event patches improve plan ranking in every counted pair; the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events. These results suggest evaluating world models for planning by where their return error occurs, in addition to how well they render frames.

    （参考文献见原文。）
