Our analysis yields two findings. First, return error concentrates at events that do not look wrong. In Fig. 1D, restoring three transitions around a Seaquest reward removes almost all return error; three random ones remove little. Across 44 reliable Atari model–collection pairs, event patches beat random patches in 39 by a median of +44 points, and the advantage appears within a few patches (Fig. 2). Event frames are rendered as well as others (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error; the same pattern holds on eighteen games added after our predictions were recorded. Second, the remaining error is structured rather than merely mistimed. Complementary patches separate errors at true events from errors elsewhere, and timing-tolerant recall shows that temporal offset explains little of the events our deterministic models miss. This structure also predicts where a diffusion model helps; event patches improve plan ranking and carry over to control tasks with rare reward events.

We summarise our contributions as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a per-transition substitution diagnostic with a budget-matched random control. It treats the world model as a black box, and we apply it to three released model families on all 26 Atari-100k games.

  • •

    We show, for the first time on released pixel world models, that return error concentrates at reward and termination transitions, also under each model’s own reward head and without the score display, and that a complementary patch separates errors at true events from other errors.

  • •

    We show that a temporal offset explains little of the events missed by deterministic models, predict all four repair outcomes with a rule recorded in advance, and show that event patches improve plan ranking in every counted pair and carry over to control tasks with rare reward events.

    • 2 Related Work

    Pixel world models support prediction and control in games [40, 10, 29, 21, 46, 66, 36, 37, 2, 12] and interactive video simulators [62, 6, 54, 60]. Yet visual fidelity can diverge from physical correctness [38] and task success [33, 64, 58]; the same disconnect appears for training likelihood [31, 13, 16], synthetic training data [1], and token pruning [57]. Concurrent work weights error by decision-relevant state dimensions [56], while DIAMOND shows that visual details matter [2]. We instead locate where decision-relevant error occurs inside a rollout.

    Oracle substitution localises such failures. Cloning Deterministic Worlds [61] substitutes true states for learned representations, while whole-model oracle interventions relate accuracy to planning [41, 49, 7]; a concurrent diagnostic uses a kinematic null [47]. Closest to ours, counterfactual debugging [32] assigns Shapley credit over time steps to a policy’s sim-to-real gap under injected faults, and agent explanations identify steps that decide a return [17, 8, 3]. We instead operate directly on released world-model rollouts, replacing individual transition pairs under a budget-matched random control. This brings perturbation-based attribution [63, 14, 44, 25], used and tested on Atari agents [15, 4], from pixels to time steps.

    Other work improves prediction with multi-step training [50, 55], goal-aware objectives [39], keyframe targets [27, 43], region- and event-aware objectives [34, 42], causal rollout structure [67], and architecture-level probing [28]. Conditional-mean effects are also studied in video prediction [35] and perception and driving models [45]. We test which explanation accounts for missed events using event survival, a diffusion model, and the same network trained deterministically.

    3 Diagnostic Setup

    The diagnostic needs only rendered frames, so it applies to released checkpoints without access to their internals.

    Return from a Predicted Trajectory.

    A probe is a real context with fixed actions a_1:H (Fig. 1A); from it, a model produces imagined observations ô_1:H. A frozen detector, shared by all world models of a game, reads each transition pair and its action as a reward sign and a termination flag, (r̂ₜ,d̂ₜ)=D(ôₜ,ôₜ₊₁,aₜ) for t

    Ĝ=∑ₜ₌₁^Hγᵗ⁻¹sgn(r̂ₜ)∏_j

    		(1)

    where G is computed in the same way from r and d, and 𝔼 averages over probes. Atari uses H=60 and γ=0.99.

    Substitutions and Their Controls.

    For channel c (observation o, reward r or termination d) and a binary mask m, let Ĝ^c,m be the return after substituting the selected real information (Fig. 1). Observation patches replace both frames of the selected transition before detection, so no pair mixes real and generated frames; unselected pairs keep their predictions. Reward and termination interventions replace r̂ or d̂. We report the fractional reduction in mean absolute return error:

    R(c,m)=1-(𝔼[|Ĝ^c,m-G|])/(𝔼[|Ĝ-G|]).

    		(2)

    The all-frame value R(o,1) measures performance when the detector sees only real transition pairs.

    The event mask starts from nonzero real reward or termination and is dilated by one step, i.e., the transitions just before and after are also selected, to cover delays in the visual markers. We report its realised coverage q=\penalty𝔼[H⁻¹∑ₜmₜ^\rmev], which includes dilation. The random mask selects the same number of steps in each rollout. The targeting advantage is

    L=R(o,m^\rmev)-R(o,m^\rmrnd).

    		(3)

    The complementary mask m̄^\rmev measures errors away from the selected events, and its contrast with the event patch classifies the failure pattern of each model.

    4 Localising the Return Error

    We localise the return error with one frozen, memoryless detector per game, shared by every world model of that game. A random patch also hits true events, and more of them as coverage grows, so the lift of Eq. (3) credits the event patch only with what it adds beyond chance.

    Figure 2 widens the event neighbourhood step by step and plots the lift against the resulting coverage. In 8 of 9 sweeps over three games and three released families, the event curve stays well above the random curve. For DIAMOND on Freeway, patching 2.8 of sixty steps removes 69% of the error, against -4% for random patches and 86% when every frame is real; on Pong, 2.1 steps remove 43% against 5%. The sweep also exposes a timing effect: without dilation the Freeway event patch is negative, consistent with the reward digit appearing after the transition that earns it, so we treat the neighbourhood as part of the measurement.

    The sweep also shows why the random control is needed. For DIAMOND and Simulus on Seaquest, both patches remove more error as coverage grows while the lift stays flat, so the event-patch reduction alone would overstate the targeting effect. Table 1 reports every game at a one-step neighbourhood, and Fig. 3 shows events beyond Atari.

    5 Missing Events and a Model-Class Repair

    Localisation shows where the return error lies, not why. We ask why imagined events are missed and whether another model class draws them.

    5.1 Absent or Mistimed Events

    A detector can miss an event in imagined frames for two reasons: the model draws it at a neighbouring step, or it does not draw it in a form the detector reads. The two predict different curves. If events are only mistimed, recall should rise with the alignment tolerance faster than for a displaced-prediction null; if they are not drawn readably, recall should stay low at every tolerance.

    5.2 A Rule Recorded Before the Outcomes

    If events are not drawn readably, a model that draws them should reduce the return error, most where the baseline misses most events. As a repair, we replace our deterministic MSE predictor with a diffusion model trained on the same data [24, 30, 2], which samples each next observation instead of regressing it (“sampling” in figures and tables). A sampled future can differ from the realised one, so we evaluate event recall, return error, and plan ranking.

    Before observing the remaining outcomes, we pre-specified this rule: a baseline event recall at τ=0 below 0.50 predicts a return-error reduction larger than the declared floor of that game, and a recall at or above 0.50 predicts no such reduction. The threshold is a heuristic for the headroom left by missing events; floors and failure conditions were fixed at the same stage. Freeway had already been scored, so the prospective score covers Pong and the three unrun sampling arms. The MSE baseline gets more training, 30k updates against 8k, because at 8k updates it detects no return on Freeway and Pong; data, sequence length, batch size, learning rate, and seeds match (supplement).

    6 Experiments

    In this section, we carry out experiments to address the following questions: Q1: Is the return error concentrated at event transitions (Sec. 6.2)? Q2: Are missed events absent or only mistimed (Sec. 6.3)? Q3: Does a diffusion model repair them as recorded (Sec. 6.4)? Q4: Do the same transitions drive plan selection (Sec. 6.5)?

    6.1 Experimental Setup

    We study 26 Atari games [5] with 64×64 observations and frameskip four, using Atari-100k [29] model checkpoints [2, 36, 12]. Across three released families and three locally trained random-policy Breakout models, 44 pairs clear reliability checks. Transfer evaluation adds 9 rows across 6 DeepMind Control tasks [51] and released iVideoGPT on robosuite [68, 60, 52].

    Atari attribution uses 400 probes, each paired with a real trajectory under the same actions. Each frozen detector must reach a reward-event F1 of 0.90 on an independent collection with environment seeds disjoint from its training data. Terminations are read but not gated; replacing them removes a median 0.7% of the return error. The real reward at the last step stays in the all-real residual (median 1.5% of the error; supplement). Figure 7 adds matched-action RSSM [20] and Transformer predictions on MiniGrid [9] and Crafter [19].

    6.2 A1: Return Error Concentrates at Events

    Main Results. As shown in Table 1, the event patch has positive lift in 39 of 44 counted pairs (sign test p=1.4×10⁻⁷), with a median of +44 points (probe-bootstrap 95% intervals: 38 above zero, 2 spanning it, 4 below). Each released family and every counted game except MsPacman has a positive median lift (per-game sign test, p=5.2×10⁻⁴); three sampling seeds change lift by a median of 2.0 points, and other discounts and horizons keep 39–41 pairs positive (supplement). As a patch changes only the selected transitions, event transitions cause most of the return error.

    Robustness to the Reward Reader. To rule out our detector, we use each model’s reward head: all 25 pairs whose head reads real futures reliably stay positive (median +46; rank correlation 0.85 with our detector), as do 6 pairs from games it cannot read. Hiding the score display keeps all 6 Pong and Freeway pairs positive (median +64; supplement).

    Comparison with Pixel Error. One may expect the error to sit in poorly rendered frames. Yet event frames are rendered as well as other frames (median ratio 0.85), and as shown in Table 2, the transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error are events only about as often as random picks, so patching them removes less than random patches. Pixel metrics thus cannot locate the return error.

    Effect of Coverage. Random patches hit more events as q grows, so a lift that only reflected sparse events would vanish. Yet the median lift is +40 above q=12% (+59 below 6%), and all Krull pairs stay positive at q=58.5%.

    Failure Patterns. With R_\rmev=R(o,m^\rmev) and the complementary patch’s R_\rmnon=R(o,m̄^\rmev), a pair is event-dominated if R_\rmev-R_\rmnon>0.20, non-event-dominated if it is below -0.20, and unclassified otherwise; the counts are 33, 5 and 6. Simulus on Freeway is event-dominated: event patches remove 72% and the complement -16%. DIAMOND on Boxing is the opposite: it imagines a return of 6.67 against a true 2.31, and event patches remove 12% and the complement 72%, so under our detector its excess return lies away from true scoring events. Under its own reward model, it is event-dominated (supplement). Most pairs thus fail by missing true events.

    6.3 A2: Missed Events Persist Under Tolerance

    We next ask whether missed events are merely mistimed (Sec. 5.1). To investigate this, we compare reward-event recall at alignment tolerance τ with a circularly displaced copy of the predictions, which keeps their event rate. If events were only mistimed, widening τ would recover most of them. As shown in Figs. 4 and 5, it recovers few: on Freeway, the MSE baseline recovers 0.091 of the events at τ=0 and 0.153 at τ=8, against 0.028 for the null, and across the five games at least 76% of its recall deficit remains at τ=8. Most missed events are thus absent rather than mistimed. DIAMOND on Freeway recovers more (0.767 to 0.932), and the diffusion model already reaches 0.943 at τ=0.

    6.4 A3: A Diffusion Model Repairs as Predicted

    If missing events cause the return error, a model that draws them should reduce it. As shown in Table 3, all four comparisons clear their floors, and the pre-specified rule scores 4/4, including 3/3 on the games whose detector passes the attribution gate. Three sampling seeds on Freeway and Pong give error ranges of 0.0356 and 0.0278, both below ΔE.

    Ablation on Sampling. A natural question is whether the gain comes from sampling. To isolate it, we train the same diffusion network with a deterministic squared-error objective (same data, 8k updates and seeds). It still has lower error than our MSE baseline on all five games and keeps Freeway’s events (recall 0.95 against 0.94); its seed-mean error is lower than with sampling on Freeway (0.096 against 0.171) and within the larger seed span on the other four, while sampling recalls more events on Pong (0.80 against 0.69; supplement). The repair thus comes from the diffusion network, not from sampling or the training loss.

    6.5 A4: Event Transitions Drive Plan Selection

    Finally, if events decide the imagined return, restoring them should also improve plan choice beyond a matched random patch. To test this, we rank eight plans from each of 150 emulator states, as a sampling-based planner does [11, 20], and score pairwise accuracy and normalised top-1 regret; 7 of the twelve pairs, including the diffusion model, pass the reliability rules (supplement), and Fig. 7 shows one. The event patch improves pairwise accuracy in all 7 pairs, whereas a random patch changes it by a median of +0.019, and median top-1 regret falls from 0.565 to 0.141. Under pre-specified rules, 15 further games add 8 pairs from Freeway, CrazyClimber and Gopher, whose detectors also pass on plan states, and the event patch improves all 8 of them (median +0.156, random +0.012; supplement). On Pong, the diffusion model raises pairwise accuracy from 0.5000 to 0.6110 (random-weighted control 0.5007). The transitions carrying the return error thus also decide plan selection.

    7 Cross-Task Transfer and Discussion

    Beyond Atari, we apply the diagnostic to six DeepMind Control tasks and robosuite, and compare matched-action rollouts on MiniGrid and Crafter (Fig. 7). On the control tasks of Fig. 3, the three comparisons whose detector passes yield +54/+54 points of lift on sparse cartpole across two architectures and +8 on ball-in-cup (supplement).

    Concurrent work finds ball disappearance and invalid ball–paddle interactions in five frozen Pong world models [34]; we locate the return error across 26 games.

    8 Conclusion

    In this paper, we introduce a per-transition substitution diagnostic that locates where the imagined return of a world model goes wrong. In 39 of 44 reliably measured model–collection pairs on Atari-100k, the return error concentrates at reward and termination transitions that pixel metrics do not single out: world models get the return wrong at events, in frames that look no worse than the rest. A rule recorded in advance predicts where a diffusion model class helps, and event patches improve plan ranking in every counted pair; the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events. These results suggest evaluating world models for planning by where their return error occurs, in addition to how well they render frames.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 神经表示也要能被光追查：NeuOctree 在稀疏八叉树角点存特征，直接预测「射线打到哪、法线与反照率」 ｜ Neural Explicit Shape Representation
item.description:
一句话：现有神经表示要么不能做显式表面查询、要么不能跨物体预测；这条把两者合到一起。

要点：

  • 问题定位：现有神经 3D 表示分别解决连续表面建模、高效图像合成或单物体压缩，但**没有同时提供光追所需的显式表面查询**与可跨物体预测的结构化输出空间
  • NeuOctree 是一种「神经显式表示」：直接预测一条射线是否命中表面、命中位置，以及该处法线与反照率
  • 实现上在稀疏八叉树体素的角点存共享特征，再插值成查询点的表示——既有显式空间结构，也保留可学习特征

为什么值得看：光追需要的是「射线求交」这种显式查询，而神经场大多只能做体积采样。把八叉树角点特征与射线级输出接起来，等于让神经表示能直接替换传统几何管线的一部分——这是 AI 表示进引擎绕不开的一步。

中文摘要：现有的神经 3D 表示各自解决一个问题：连续表面建模、高效图像合成或单物体压缩；但没有一种同时提供光追所需的显式表面查询，以及能跨物体预测的结构化输出空间。NeuOctree 因此提出一种「神经显式表示」：它直接预测一条射线是否命中表面、命中在哪里，以及该点的法线与反照率。实现方式是在稀疏八叉树的体素角点存储共享特征，并把它们插值成查询位置的表示，从而既保留显式的空间结构，又保留可学习特征的表达力。对渲染管线来说，这意味着神经表示第一次有资格直接承担「射线求交」这一环，而不只是做体积采样。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-11-02

Neural Explicit Shape Representation

Abstract

Existing neural 3D representations separately address continuous surface modeling, efficient image synthesis, or object-specific compression. They do not jointly provide the explicit surface queries required by ray tracing and a structured output space that can be predicted across objects. We introduce NeuOctree, a neural explicit representation that directly predicts whether and where a ray intersects a surface, together with its normal and albedo. NeuOctree stores shared features at the corners of sparse octree voxels and interpolates them into a continuous local field. A lightweight decoder with recurrent intersection-guided sampling refines each query near the predicted surface, enabling direct surface rendering without mesh extraction or texture baking and accommodating open, non-watertight geometry. The same octree structure supports both compact per-object optimization and a shared octree CNN that constructs renderable assets from colored point clouds without per-object fitting. Across seven meshes and four storage budgets, NeuOctree achieves the lowest positional error in 24 of 28 comparisons while retaining competitive normal accuracy, and substantially improves joint geometry–appearance reconstruction over N-BVH and VQAD. The feedforward model constructs a representation in 0.05 seconds and transfers from Objaverse to ShapeNet without retraining. We further demonstrate ray-traced rendering and image-conditioned generation, showing that NeuOctree provides a common output space for neural inference and direct surface rendering. Code is available at https://github.com/octree-nn/neural-octree.

1 Introduction

Learning compact 3D assets requires a representation that connects neural prediction with geometric computation. A ray-tracing renderer needs to determine where a ray intersects an object and recover the normal and material attributes at that point. A network trained across objects benefits from a structured output space in which to predict geometry and appearance. Bringing these requirements together would allow learned assets to pass directly from a neural network to a ray-tracing renderer.

Existing representations address different parts of this problem. Signed distance fields [(Park et al., 2019; Chabra et al., 2020)] and occupancy fields [(Mescheder et al., 2019)] encode surfaces as level sets of learned scalar functions. NeRF [(Mildenhall et al., 2020)] jointly models density and radiance, with hash encodings [(Müller et al., 2022)] and sparse voxel structures [(Yu et al., 2021; Fridovich-Keil et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020b)] reducing the cost of field evaluation and rendering. SDF-based volume rendering [(Wang et al., 2021)] improves surface reconstruction, while Gaussian splatting and sparse voxel rasterization [(Huang et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025)] enable efficient image synthesis. These advances illustrate the value of compact, spatially organized representations. However, density or occupancy values do not directly specify the intersection and material attributes required by a surface ray tracer: these quantities must be recovered through additional surface localization or geometry extraction.

Neural compression methods bring learned representations closer to conventional surface rendering. Neural Geometry Fields [(Sivaram et al., 2024)] encode detailed geometry through displacements of coarse mesh patches, while N-BVH [(Weier et al., 2024)] directly predicts ray intersections and appearance within a bounding volume hierarchy. Both construct their representations through object-specific optimization. Building on the direct ray-query interface, we seek a representation whose geometry and appearance can also be predicted by a shared network across objects.

We introduce NeuOctree, a neural explicit shape representation that couples direct ray–surface intersection prediction with an octree-based sparse voxel structure. The octree organizes local geometry, skips empty space during traversal, and provides a structured domain for 3D neural networks. Adjacent voxels share corner features, defining a continuous feature field through trilinear interpolation. A lightweight, shared MLP decodes the ray and interpolated features into a hit probability, intersection position, surface normal, and albedo. These outputs supply the surface queries needed for ray tracing without mesh extraction or texture baking. Because the representation does not require an inside–outside labeling, it also accommodates open, non-watertight surfaces.

Accurate intersection prediction requires querying the right part of the feature field. Features sampled only at a voxel’s boundary may be far from the surface, and rays observing the same surface point can enter the voxel at different locations. We therefore introduce a recurrent sampling strategy that uses predicted intersections to guide subsequent feature queries. This refinement brings queries closer to the surface and encourages rays from different views to access features near the same location. The ablation shows improved intersection and normal accuracy over endpoint-only and uniform sampling.

The same structure enables us to amortize representation construction across objects. We build a feedforward 3D U-Net on octree-based CNNs [(Wang et al., 2017)] to predict voxel-corner features from colored point clouds. Averaging predictions at shared vertices produces a consistent feature field, which is decoded by the shared intersection MLP. Training the feature extractor and decoder jointly with rendering losses allows a single checkpoint to construct geometry and appearance for new inputs without per-object optimization. NeuOctree thus supports both per-object compression and feedforward construction within the same representation and renderer.

We evaluate per-object compression on seven meshes from Thingi10K and the Stanford 3D Scanning Repository at four storage budgets. NeuOctree achieves the lowest positional error in 24 of 28 model–budget comparisons and competitive normal accuracy compared with geometry-only methods, and significantly overperforms N-BVH and VQAD which jointly represent geometry and appearance. On the separate feedforward task, a shared checkpoint constructs a representation in 0.05 seconds with lower intersection error, compared with approximately 3.5 minutes for N-BVH fitting under the reported settings. The same checkpoint, trained on Objaverse, transfers to ShapeNet without retraining. We further demonstrate direct ray-traced rendering with reshading, reflection, refraction, and fisheye projection, and show image-conditioned generation of NeuOctree assets as a downstream application. Our contributions are:

  • -

    A structured neural surface representation that jointly encodes geometry and appearance in shared voxel-corner features and supports direct ray-traced rendering.

  • -

    Recurrent intersection refinement that adaptively queries the continuous feature field to improve the accuracy of predicted surface intersections and normals.

  • -

    Feedforward representation construction that predicts renderable NeuOctree assets without per-object optimization, with demonstrated transfer across datasets and native 3D generation as a downstream application.

    • 2 Related Work

    Neural Surface and Radiance Representations.

    Neural implicit fields provide a compact and differentiable alternative to explicit geometry. Early methods represented shapes with coordinate-based multilayer perceptrons, using signed distance functions (SDFs) [(Park et al., 2019; Chabra et al., 2020)] or occupancy fields [(Mescheder et al., 2019)]. Subsequent approaches introduced octrees and adaptive spatial partitions [(Takikawa et al., 2021; Martel et al., 2021)], while neural radiance fields jointly modeled density and appearance through volume rendering [(Mildenhall et al., 2020)]. Octree and hash-grid variants [(Yu et al., 2021; Fridovich-Keil et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020b; Müller et al., 2022)], SDF–density hybrids [(Wang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023)], and explicit rasterization-based representations [(Huang et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025)] have substantially improved memory use or image-rendering speed.

    These methods nevertheless expose a mismatch with surface ray tracing. A density or occupancy value does not directly specify a ray–surface intersection, normal, or material; obtaining these quantities typically requires repeated field evaluations, surface localization, or mesh extraction. The resulting geometric ambiguity can compromise fine detail, and level-set formulations often rely on an inside–outside convention that is awkward for open or non-watertight surfaces. NeuOctree instead makes the ray–surface query the representation’s primary interface: a shared decoder predicts the hit, position, normal, and albedo from a ray and a continuous octree feature field. This design preserves the compactness of neural representations while enabling direct ray-traced rendering without an intermediate mesh or texture-baking stage.

    Neural Mesh Compression.

    Traditional mesh compression combines connectivity coding, coordinate quantization, and simplification to reduce storage while preserving surface fidelity [(Deering, 1995; Chow, 1997; Diaz-Gutierrez et al., 2005; Touma & Gotsman, 1998; Heckbert & Garland, 1999)]. Learning-based methods replace hand-designed operators with graph networks or lightweight MLPs that upsample a coarse mesh and predict vertex displacements [(Liu et al., 2020a; Chen et al., 2023; Sivaram et al., 2024; Pentapati et al., 2025)]. Although effective for individual assets, these approaches are generally optimized per mesh, focus primarily on geometry, and require a fixed coarse topology; appearance is commonly handled by a separate texture-baking step. N-BVH [(Weier et al., 2024)] is closer to our setting because it predicts ray intersections and appearance within a hierarchical structure, but it also relies on object-specific optimization.

    NeuOctree addresses these limitations with a sparse octree that supplies a global spatial prior and shared voxel-corner features that provide local context. Geometry and appearance are decoded through the same ray-query interface, so the representation can be optimized as a compact per-object asset or predicted by a shared network across objects. The distinction is therefore not only a different compression structure, but also a shift from per-mesh fitting to a renderable representation that supports feedforward construction.

    Structured 3D Learning and Feedforward Reconstruction.

    Point-, voxel-, and sparse-voxel networks have become standard tools for 3D perception and generation [(Qi et al., 2017a; Qi et al., 2017b; Li et al., 2018; Maturana & Scherer, 2015; Wu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017; Graham et al., 2018; Choy et al., 2019; Wang, 2023; Wu et al., 2024)]. Their structured spatial domains support scalable feature extraction, but their outputs are typically occupancies, semantic features, or task-specific predictions rather than a representation that can be queried directly by a surface renderer. NeuOctree uses the same structured prior for a different purpose: an octree U-Net predicts features at voxel corners from colored point clouds, and averaging shared vertices yields a consistent continuous field for the ray-intersection decoder. This establishes a direct bridge between feedforward 3D learning and surface rendering: one shared checkpoint constructs geometry and appearance without per-object optimization, while the resulting representation remains suitable for ray tracing and can serve as a native output space for 3D generation.

    3 Method

    Overview.

    NeuOctree is built around a direct surface query. An asset is represented by an occupied sparse octree and a continuous feature field defined on its voxel corners. Given a ray segment inside an occupied voxel, a shared decoder predicts whether the ray hits the surface and, if so, the intersection position, normal, and albedo. The same decoder is used for every voxel and every ray; only the octree topology and its feature values vary across assets. This separation lets us use the representation in two regimes: a feature table can be optimized for one asset, or an octree network can predict the feature field in a single feedforward pass. In both cases the output is directly consumable by a surface ray tracer and does not require mesh extraction or texture baking.

    3.1 Structured Neural Surface Representation

    Sparse octree and continuous feature field.

    We construct an octree from the input point cloud and retain its occupied leaf voxels. The octree provides a structured support for spatial queries and lets the renderer skip empty space. For an occupied voxel v, let {f_v,ijk}_i,j,k∈{0,1} denote its eight corner features. At a local coordinate q∈[0,1]³, the decoder reads the continuous feature field by trilinear interpolation,

    φᵥ(q)=∑_i,j,k∈{0,1}wᵢⱼₖ(q) f_v,ijk,

    where wᵢⱼₖ are the standard trilinear weights. Corner features shared by adjacent voxels are identified as one vertex feature, so interpolation remains continuous across voxel boundaries. In per-object optimization, the unique vertex features are learned directly. In the feedforward model, the network first predicts eight corner slots for each occupied voxel; slots that refer to the same geometric vertex are averaged before rendering. This deterministic aggregation converts voxel outputs into the same shared feature field used by the optimized representation.

    For the colored feedforward setting, the interpolated field can be augmented with a voxel-local residual feature. We optionally use a pooled input-color prior in the material branch. These terms provide local appearance context without changing the surface-query interface or shared vertex field.

    Ray-query decoder.

    For a ray traversing voxel v, we denote the local entry and exit points by pᵢₙ and pₒᵤₜ, and use d=norm(pₒᵤₜ-pᵢₙ) as the local ray direction. At a query position q, a geometry branch receives the interpolated feature, the local position, the ray direction, and the current refinement state. A separate material branch uses the same spatial feature field and ray information together with the current position and color state. Both branches are lightweight residual MLPs whose weights are shared across all voxels and rays. Their outputs are

    (a,z,sₕ)=G_θ(φᵥ(q),q,d,state), c=σ (M_θ(φᵥ(q),q,d,state)),

    where a∈ℝ³ parameterizes the position, z∈ℝ³ is normalized to produce the surface normal, sₕ is the hit logit, and σ is the sigmoid function. The predicted hit probability is h=σ(sₕ) and the predicted albedo is c∈[0,1]³.

    The position parameterization is ray-local. In the segment-bounded variant used by the feedforward rendering configuration, the first component of σ(a) gives α∈[0,1] and

    p̂=pᵢₙ+α(pₒᵤₜ-pᵢₙ).

    The per-object geometry compression protocol uses the equivalent ray-projection parameterization, which projects the predicted local point onto the current ray line. When the segment-bounded option is enabled, this projection is restricted to the current segment. Both forms preserve the key property that the decoder predicts a surface intersection rather than a density level set. Fourier position features are not used in the reported configurations.

    3.2 Recurrent Intersection Refinement

    Samples taken only at a voxel boundary can be far from the surface, and the boundary point depends on viewing direction even when rays observe the same surface point. A single boundary query therefore makes the decoder learn an unnecessarily view-dependent mapping. We use the predicted intersection to place later queries in the continuous feature field.

    Let qₖ be the k-th adaptive query. The decoder produces an intersection estimate p̂ₖ and the next query is obtained by projecting this estimate back onto the current ray parameterization,

    qₖ₊₁=Π_ray(p̂ₖ),

    where Π_ray denotes ray-line projection or its segment-bounded variant, depending on the chosen position parameterization. The recurrent decoder can maintain a chained hidden state across iterations. Our pooled variant, used for the reported compression and sampling experiments, encodes the entry and exit points as ordinary members of the feature set, initializes the first interior query at the segment midpoint, and then adds further adaptively placed queries from the preceding readout. The per-query hidden increments are averaged before a shared output head predicts the final attributes. With three adaptive iterations this gives five feature reads per voxel segment (entry, exit, and three adaptive queries). The fixed-sampling ablations use the same decoder modules and replace only the adaptive positions with predetermined positions.

    This construction couples all queries to the same local feature field while moving later queries toward the surface. It therefore improves localization and normal prediction without introducing a large per-voxel network or requiring volume samples along the entire ray. When the chained recurrent variant is used, intermediate predictions are also supervised; at inference we use the final stage.

    3.3 Octree Traversal and Surface Rendering

    Given a camera ray, we enumerate its intersections with occupied leaf voxels in front-to-back order. Each candidate is represented by its local entry and exit points and the index of its voxel feature block. The decoder is evaluated on these candidates in chunks. A candidate is accepted when its hit probability exceeds a threshold; the first accepted candidate for each ray is selected. Its local position is converted back to octree coordinates by adding the voxel origin, while the predicted normal and albedo are retained as surface attributes. Rays for which no candidate is accepted return the background value. Thus octree traversal replaces the broad volume sampling used by neural radiance fields, and the selected attributes can be passed directly to a standard ray-tracing integrator for reshading, reflection, refraction, or other camera effects.

    3.4 Feedforward Representation Construction

    The structured representation makes feature construction amortizable across objects. We build an input octree from a colored point cloud and attach point color, local point offset, and normalized global coordinates to occupied cells. An octree-based U-Net [(Wang et al., 2017)] processes this sparse hierarchy with octree convolutions, downsampling and upsampling stages, residual blocks, and skip connections. At the query depth, it predicts a tensor with eight feature slots per occupied voxel. Reshaping these slots and averaging all slots that share a geometric vertex yields the continuous field used by the decoder.

    The feature extractor and the ray-query decoder are trained jointly with the same rendering losses used for per-object optimization. Consequently, a single checkpoint maps a new colored point cloud to a renderable NeuOctree without optimizing the object-specific feature table. The resulting field is also a native output space for the image-conditioned generation pipeline in Section 4.3.

    3.5 Training Objective

    Training supervision is obtained by unprojecting RGB–D images into camera rays. For every occupied ray–voxel segment before the ground-truth surface, we store a hit label, the local intersection position, the oriented normal, and the albedo. Let m denote the hit label and let ℙ be the positive surface pairs. The pointwise objective is

    L_PNCH=Lₚ(ℙ)+Lₙ(ℙ)+λₕLₕᵢₜ(h,m)+λ_cL_color(c,c^*;ℙ),

    where Lₚ and Lₙ are position and normal reconstruction losses, Lₕᵢₜ is BCE (or its class-balanced variant), and L_color is a relative color reconstruction loss. The geometry terms are masked by the ground-truth hit labels; in the feedforward configuration their normalization is restricted to positive surface pairs so that empty ray–voxel segments do not dilute the surface signal.

    For colored reconstruction, we supplement the pointwise terms with image-level normal and albedo SSIM losses, together with optional smoothness, color constancy, detail-gradient, and hit-topology regularizers. In compact form,

    L=∑ₖwₖ(L_PNCH⁽ᵏ⁾+λ_imgL_img⁽ᵏ⁾+λₜₒₚₒLₜₒₚₒ⁽ᵏ⁾), ∑ₖwₖ=1,

    where k indexes recurrent stages. Image terms are masked by valid surface pixels when configured, while hit-topology terms penalize holes, floaters, and boundary inconsistencies. Geometry-only experiments use the corresponding subset to supervise the renderer.

    4 Results

    4.1 Results of Per-Mesh Compression

    We compare NeuOctree with the per-object optimization methods NGF [(Sivaram et al., 2024)], QNDF [(Pentapati et al., 2025)], VQAD [(Takikawa et al., 2022)], and N-BVH [(Weier et al., 2024)] over a broad range of storage budgets. VQAD is adapted to predict surface normals and intersection positions under the same geometry supervision.

    Dataset and Metrics.

    We evaluate the seven meshes in Table1 from the Stanford 3D Scanning Repository [(Stanford University, 1994)] and Thingi10K [(Zhou & Jacobson, 2016)], rendering 16 fixed 512×512 views. We report mean ray–surface position error dₚₘ in normalized object coordinates, scaled by 10³, and oriented normal error dₙₒᵣₘ in degrees.

    Geometry Compression.

    As shown in Table1, NeuOctree obtains the lowest dₚₘ in 24 of 28 model–budget comparisons. It wins all 21 at 81–244 KiB and three of seven at 823 KiB, where QNDF takes the other four. NeuOctree also wins 12 normal-error comparisons; NGF leads mainly at the smallest payload, while QNDF is competitive only at the largest. Thus, the strongest baseline changes with payload, whereas NeuOctree maintains the most consistent positional accuracy. The curves in Fig.4 and qualitative results in Fig.3 corroborate this trend, showing cleaner silhouettes and better preservation of fine structures.

    Joint Geometry and Appearance Compression.

    On Objaverse, per-object NeuOctree achieves the best normal accuracy and PSNR; on ShapeNet, it is best on all three metrics in Table3. Relative to VQAD, it reduces dₚₘ and dₙₒᵣₘ by 85.5% and 37.8% on Objaverse while adding 1.11 dB PSNR. The ShapeNet improvements are 95.8%, 32.6%, and 9.33 dB, respectively. Representative albedo reconstructions are shown in Fig.5.

    Sampling Strategy Ablation.

    We compare recurrent sampling with endpoint-only and four-sample uniform variants. Recurrent sampling reduces dₚₘ and dₙₒᵣₘ by 7.7% and 9.4% relative to uniform sampling, and by 12.0% and 17.0% relative to endpoint-only sampling. This supports querying the feature field near the predicted surface rather than at fixed locations.

    Open-Surface Reconstruction.

    We evaluate NeuOctree and VQAD on an open glass pane using an 823 KiB budget. For matched mirrored face-on cameras, we back-project both depth maps and measure their separation dz along the pane normal at pixels visible from both sides (Fig.6). NeuOctree matches the GT median dz=0, whereas VQAD gives dz=0.059 world units, revealing a systematic two-sided offset. These results support NeuOctree’s ability to represent open surfaces without an inside–outside labeling like VQAD.

    4.2 Results of Feedforward Methods

    Dataset and Metrics.

    Our feedforward model is trained on a randomly sampled subset of Objaverse with 32k assets. We evaluate on 30 unseen Objaverse assets and 30 ShapeNet assets to compare with per-object methods. The same metrics dₚₘ, dₙₒᵣₘ as in Section4.1 are used, along with PSNR for appearance reconstruction.

    Evaluation.

    We evaluate a shared feedforward checkpoint under the same rendering and scoring protocol used for the per-object methods. Ours-F retains the direct ray-query interface without per-object fitting. On Objaverse, its reconstruction is comparable to VQAD: it has substantially lower positional error, while VQAD remains stronger on normal accuracy and PSNR. On ShapeNet, Ours-F improves all three reported metrics over VQAD, showing that the same structured output space remains effective after the dataset shift.

    Efficiency.

    Table3 reports practical fitting times of each method. N-BVH requires about 3 minutes and VQAD requires tens of minutes of optimization for each object. In contrast, our feedforward model constructs a renderable representation from a colored point cloud in 50 ms with 19.5 hours for training paid once across all objects. As shown in Table3, this removes per-object optimization while retaining competitive reconstruction quality.

    Generalization.

    The shared model is trained on Objaverse and evaluated on ShapeNet without retraining. Despite this distribution shift, our feedforward model outperforms both VQAD and N-BVH on ShapeNet, although both baselines optimize each object separately. This result shows that the octree feature extractor and intersection decoder transfer across datasets while preserving the directly renderable output space.

    4.3 Applications

    Photorealistic Rendering with Ray Tracing.

    Since the decoder returns a hit, position, normal, and albedo, NeuOctree can be queried directly by a surface ray tracer. It supports reshading, reflection, refraction, and a fisheye projection without mesh extraction or texture baking (Fig.7).

    Native 3D Generation.

    NeuOctree can also serve as the native output of an image-conditioned generator. A sparse-octree VAE compresses node features, and a flow-matching DiT predicts occupancy and latent features that decode directly into renderable geometry and appearance. Each example in Fig.8 shows the conditioning image, surface normal, and albedo.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented NeuOctree, a neural explicit surface representation for ray tracing. Shared corner features in a sparse octree and a recurrent decoder jointly predict ray–surface hits, positions, normals, and albedo, supporting compact geometry–appearance modeling, direct rendering, and open surfaces. Experiments show accurate reconstruction across meshes and budgets; the shared feedforward model constructs a renderable representation in about 50 ms, rather than minutes of per-object optimization, and transfers from Objaverse to ShapeNet without retraining. Ray-traced rendering and image-conditioned generation further demonstrate the versatility of this structured output space.

    NeuOctree still requires costly high-fidelity per-object fitting and models albedo rather than view-dependent materials; generation remains a proof of concept. Future work will accelerate octree construction, extend surface queries to richer materials, lighting, and dynamics, and develop NeuOctree as a native output space for 3D generative models.

    AI use statement

    In this work, we used a generative AI coding assistant to assist with limited code debugging, migrate the existing manuscript into the ICLR 2027 LaTeX template, proofread the language, and check compilation and formatting. It was not used to produce the research ideas, experimental results, figures, or scientific claims in this paper. The authors reviewed the revised source and take responsibility for the final content of this work.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Experimental Details and Additional Results

    This appendix records the configurations that determine the entries in the main paper, with particular emphasis on the capacity-matched comparison in Table1. We separate the per-object optimization setting from the shared feedforward model because their stored state and training protocols are fundamentally different.

    A.1 Common Evaluation Protocol

    Objects and cameras.

    The geometry-compression benchmark contains Armadillo, Buddha, Dragon, Einstein, Lucy, Metatron, and XYZ-Dragon. Every method is scored from the same 16 fixed cameras at 512×512 resolution, with a 60^∘ field of view and a camera distance of 2.5 after normalizing the longest bounding-box edge to 2. We use the same per-object coordinate convention and camera conversion for all methods.

    Metrics.

    The evaluation mask is the union of the ground-truth and predicted foreground masks. The position metric dₚₘ is the mean Euclidean distance between corresponding ray intersections in normalized object coordinates and is reported after multiplication by 10³. The normal metric dₙₒᵣₘ is the mean oriented angular error in degrees. Appearance experiments additionally report RGB PSNR. Some evaluation implementations store dₚₘ after multiplication by 10⁴; those values are divided by ten before insertion into the paper.

    Payload accounting.

    The four nominal targets are 82,944, 124,928, 249,856, and 842,752 bytes, reported as 81, 122, 244, and 823 KiB. A payload includes all object-specific state required by a method at inference time. Shared weights of the feedforward model are excluded from its per-object representation size. The tables below record the actual configuration and measured payload used for each of the 28 cells of every method. We use the abbreviations D (octree depth), F (feature dimension or requested/coarse faces, as specified by the caption), H (decoder width), L (octree level), B (codebook bit width), Q (coarse quads), N (BVH nodes), and P (measured payload in bytes).

    A.2 Feedforward NeuOctree

    Input representation and architecture.

    The reported feedforward model is the depth-9 union variant. For each object, its input octree is the union of a conservatively rasterized depth-9 mesh occupancy (with colors sampled from eight rendered albedo views) and a 200k point cloud. The union is capped at 900,000 depth-9 cells; this cap limits the encoder memory without changing the depth-7 coverage used by the renderer. The octree uses full_depth=4 and query depth 7. Its nine LPF input channels encode position, within-cell offset, and local color. A sparse octree U-Net maps the depth-9 input to 128 channels at query depth 7. These channels are reshaped into eight 16-dimensional corner features per voxel and averaged at shared corners, yielding the continuous vertex feature field used by the renderer. The renderer has hidden width 128, four recurrent refinements, 8-dimensional voxel features, RMSNorm, and segment-position encoding. Its hit threshold is 0.4, and the forward pass is chunked at 65,536 candidates (with a maximum render batch of 262,144 queries).

    Figure 9 details the 3D U-Net used by the feedforward encoder. The sparse octree input and point-cloud features enter a multiscale encoder, are fused at the bottleneck, and are decoded with skip connections to produce the output octree and point features. Each octree residual block uses two 1×1 convolutions with RMSNorm and ReLU, followed by a residual addition and a final ReLU, as shown in the lower panel.

    Losses.

    The hit term uses balanced binary cross-entropy with positive weight 1.5, Tversky weight 0.2 and (α,β,γ)=(0.3,0.7,1.0). Hole, floater, and boundary penalties have weights 0.1, 0.1, and 0.2. Color uses weight 2.0, a Charbonnier penalty, gradient weight 0.2, and masked SSIM weight 0.5. Normal supervision uses cosine weight 0.1, gradient weight 0.3, and masked SSIM weight 0.3. We additionally use parameter ℓ₂ regularization of 10⁻³, ray-distance weight 0.5, final-stage weight 0.5, and detail scale 4.0.

    Training and inference time.

    The reported d9-union model was selected on the full 1,000-object validation set with a selection score of 1.3781. It was trained from random initialization for three epochs (180,000 optimizer steps) on four RTX 3090 GPUs, corresponding to approximately 50.6 h of uninterrupted training. Building the depth-9 occupancy cache is a separate one-time cost of approximately 5.2 h and 91 GB. The 19.5 h figure in the main paper is the eight-GPU equivalent estimated from measured per-iteration throughput. These training costs are not comparable to the per-object timing table. Inference timing excludes data loading, rendering, and metric evaluation.

    Stored representation size.

    The shared feedforward network has 36.888M parameters and is not replicated per object. Per-object state consists of depth-7 topology, a 16-dimensional fp16 vertex field, and an optional 8-dimensional fp16 voxel field. The 128-channel U-Net output is an intermediate tensor and is not stored. With the voxel field enabled, the seven reference objects occupy 381–1,674 KiB (806 KiB on average); without it, they occupy 304–1,372 KiB (654 KiB on average).

    A.3 Complete Capacity Configurations for Table 1

    NeuOctree (per-object optimization).

    For every cell, we optimize a geometry-only NeuOctree for 300 epochs over 242 training views, using two RTX 4090 GPUs with pair-balanced DDP. The optimizer uses an initial learning rate of 2×10⁻³ with linear decay to 10⁻⁵. We use three decoder refinements, recurrent-pool sampling, no voxel-feature branch, and fp16 storage. Each entry below is D/F/H followed by the measured payload. The feature dimension and decoder width are jointly selected to fill the target budget; consequently, they vary across both objects and rates. Table5 reports the complete settings.

    NGF.

    We keep the upstream NGF network fixed (20 features, eight Fourier-feature levels, batch size 10, and a fixed seed); only the coarse quad mesh changes the object-specific payload. Training uses four resolution levels, 100 iterations per level, batch size 10, and 200 reference views on one RTX 4090. Each entry in Table7 is requested faces F, realized coarse quads Q, and measured payload P. The paper metrics are recomputed with the common 16-view union-mask evaluator, not NGF’s native held-out-view evaluator.

    QNDF.

    QNDF is run for 4,000 optimizer iterations on one RTX 4090. Its size is controlled by the realized coarse-mesh face count F and decoder width H. Entries in Table7 are F/H and measured payload. The Dragon 823 KiB cell is an exception: a request for 1,900 faces produced a remeshed surface with 12,798 faces and 6,381 vertices, explaining its larger run time relative to the other cells at this rate.

    VQAD.

    We adapt VQAD to six-channel geometry supervision (normal and normalized position), use four LODs, and optimize for 100 epochs over 242 training views with RMSprop at 10⁻³ and AMP. Table 1 uses the actual evaluated configuration for each cell: two 81 KiB cells use the final 3-bit setting, 13 further cells use uniform splitting, and the remaining cells use the settings listed in Table9. Entries are L/B/F/H/K, where K is the number of decoder layers, followed by payload P.

    N-BVH.

    N-BVH uses four features per level, eight levels, 64 neurons, four hidden layers, WorldT depth learning, a last split at iteration 3,000, split and split-interval scale factors of 2, and 10,000 training steps on one RTX 4090. The hash-map sizes are 2⁹, 2⁹, 2¹⁰, and 2¹¹ across the four rates. Capacity is controlled by split intervals 235, 100, 60, and 28, producing the node counts in Table9. Entries are node count N and payload P.

    A.4 Training Hardware and Runtime

    All per-object timing runs were executed on the same RTX 4090 server. Ours uses two GPUs with DDP; each baseline uses one GPU. The values in Table10 are wall-clock minutes per object, averaged over all seven meshes. They are practical end-to-end fitting costs under each method’s own training budget, rather than equal-GPU or equal-step throughput measurements. The N-BVH times exclude the separate capacity-calibration probe. The VQAD timing sweep uses a uniform 65,536-sample protocol for all 28 cells; its timing configurations may therefore differ from the quality configurations in Table9.

    Feedforward training uses four RTX 3090 GPUs. The capacity and timing experiments use the GPU allocations reported in Table10, and the generation experiments use four RTX 5090 GPUs. We report only the devices allocated to each experiment rather than the total capacity of the host.

    A.5 Native 3D Generation Details

    The generation demonstration uses NeuOctree itself as the output domain. A sparse-octree VAE encodes the occupancy and feature tensors of a renderable NeuOctree into an 8³ latent grid. An image-conditioned flow-matching DiT predicts both latent features and occupancy; the VAE decoder then reconstructs the octree feature field, which can be queried by the same surface renderer as the reconstructed assets. No mesh extraction or post-hoc texture baking is required, and the paper does not use this experiment for a quantitative comparison with external generation systems.

    The generation setup uses 5,000 ShapeNet objects from ten categories. The VAE receives a 128³ representation, downsamples it four times to 8³, and uses a latent dimension of 32. It is trained with AdamW (learning rate 10⁻⁴, weight decay 0.01), batch size 32, on four RTX 5090 GPUs. For the image-conditioned model, 16 random Blender views are rendered per asset, with one retained for testing. The DiT has approximately 0.7B parameters: width 1,536, 16 transformer blocks, 12 attention heads, and MLP width 8,192. It uses the same optimizer settings, batch size 16, and four RTX 5090 GPUs.

    A.6 Reproducibility Notes and Limitations

    The capacity tables report measured payloads rather than inferring size from a compression-ratio label. The actual capacity controls are the values in Tables5, 7, 7, 9 and 9. The VQAD quality table uses the tested configuration listed for each cell, whereas its timing table uses a uniform 28-cell protocol. QNDF’s Dragon 823 KiB remeshing exception and N-BVH’s excluded calibration probe are disclosed above. Finally, the feedforward inference time measures representation construction only; image rendering and evaluation are separate downstream operations.

    A.7 Additional Qualitative Results

    Figure11 supplies the four Table 1 objects not shown in the main qualitative compression figure. The N-BVH render uses its method background, which is retained rather than cosmetically altered.

    Figure11 shows seven further Objaverse objects under a matched view. NeuOctree-F preserves large color regions and thin structures without per-object fitting; VQAD is often similarly sharp, whereas N-BVH more frequently exhibits color fragmentation or smoothing at the same nominal 823 KiB budget.

一句话：现有神经表示要么不能做显式表面查询、要么不能跨物体预测；这条把两者合到一起。

要点：

  • 问题定位：现有神经 3D 表示分别解决连续表面建模、高效图像合成或单物体压缩，但**没有同时提供光追所需的显式表面查询**与可跨物体预测的结构化输出空间
  • NeuOctree 是一种「神经显式表示」：直接预测一条射线是否命中表面、命中位置，以及该处法线与反照率
  • 实现上在稀疏八叉树体素的角点存共享特征，再插值成查询点的表示——既有显式空间结构，也保留可学习特征

为什么值得看：光追需要的是「射线求交」这种显式查询，而神经场大多只能做体积采样。把八叉树角点特征与射线级输出接起来，等于让神经表示能直接替换传统几何管线的一部分——这是 AI 表示进引擎绕不开的一步。

中文摘要：现有的神经 3D 表示各自解决一个问题：连续表面建模、高效图像合成或单物体压缩；但没有一种同时提供光追所需的显式表面查询，以及能跨物体预测的结构化输出空间。NeuOctree 因此提出一种「神经显式表示」：它直接预测一条射线是否命中表面、命中在哪里，以及该点的法线与反照率。实现方式是在稀疏八叉树的体素角点存储共享特征，并把它们插值成查询位置的表示，从而既保留显式的空间结构，又保留可学习特征的表达力。对渲染管线来说，这意味着神经表示第一次有资格直接承担「射线求交」这一环，而不只是做体积采样。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-11-02

Neural Explicit Shape Representation

Abstract

Existing neural 3D representations separately address continuous surface modeling, efficient image synthesis, or object-specific compression. They do not jointly provide the explicit surface queries required by ray tracing and a structured output space that can be predicted across objects. We introduce NeuOctree, a neural explicit representation that directly predicts whether and where a ray intersects a surface, together with its normal and albedo. NeuOctree stores shared features at the corners of sparse octree voxels and interpolates them into a continuous local field. A lightweight decoder with recurrent intersection-guided sampling refines each query near the predicted surface, enabling direct surface rendering without mesh extraction or texture baking and accommodating open, non-watertight geometry. The same octree structure supports both compact per-object optimization and a shared octree CNN that constructs renderable assets from colored point clouds without per-object fitting. Across seven meshes and four storage budgets, NeuOctree achieves the lowest positional error in 24 of 28 comparisons while retaining competitive normal accuracy, and substantially improves joint geometry–appearance reconstruction over N-BVH and VQAD. The feedforward model constructs a representation in 0.05 seconds and transfers from Objaverse to ShapeNet without retraining. We further demonstrate ray-traced rendering and image-conditioned generation, showing that NeuOctree provides a common output space for neural inference and direct surface rendering. Code is available at https://github.com/octree-nn/neural-octree.

1 Introduction

Learning compact 3D assets requires a representation that connects neural prediction with geometric computation. A ray-tracing renderer needs to determine where a ray intersects an object and recover the normal and material attributes at that point. A network trained across objects benefits from a structured output space in which to predict geometry and appearance. Bringing these requirements together would allow learned assets to pass directly from a neural network to a ray-tracing renderer.

Existing representations address different parts of this problem. Signed distance fields [(Park et al., 2019; Chabra et al., 2020)] and occupancy fields [(Mescheder et al., 2019)] encode surfaces as level sets of learned scalar functions. NeRF [(Mildenhall et al., 2020)] jointly models density and radiance, with hash encodings [(Müller et al., 2022)] and sparse voxel structures [(Yu et al., 2021; Fridovich-Keil et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020b)] reducing the cost of field evaluation and rendering. SDF-based volume rendering [(Wang et al., 2021)] improves surface reconstruction, while Gaussian splatting and sparse voxel rasterization [(Huang et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025)] enable efficient image synthesis. These advances illustrate the value of compact, spatially organized representations. However, density or occupancy values do not directly specify the intersection and material attributes required by a surface ray tracer: these quantities must be recovered through additional surface localization or geometry extraction.

Neural compression methods bring learned representations closer to conventional surface rendering. Neural Geometry Fields [(Sivaram et al., 2024)] encode detailed geometry through displacements of coarse mesh patches, while N-BVH [(Weier et al., 2024)] directly predicts ray intersections and appearance within a bounding volume hierarchy. Both construct their representations through object-specific optimization. Building on the direct ray-query interface, we seek a representation whose geometry and appearance can also be predicted by a shared network across objects.

We introduce NeuOctree, a neural explicit shape representation that couples direct ray–surface intersection prediction with an octree-based sparse voxel structure. The octree organizes local geometry, skips empty space during traversal, and provides a structured domain for 3D neural networks. Adjacent voxels share corner features, defining a continuous feature field through trilinear interpolation. A lightweight, shared MLP decodes the ray and interpolated features into a hit probability, intersection position, surface normal, and albedo. These outputs supply the surface queries needed for ray tracing without mesh extraction or texture baking. Because the representation does not require an inside–outside labeling, it also accommodates open, non-watertight surfaces.

Accurate intersection prediction requires querying the right part of the feature field. Features sampled only at a voxel’s boundary may be far from the surface, and rays observing the same surface point can enter the voxel at different locations. We therefore introduce a recurrent sampling strategy that uses predicted intersections to guide subsequent feature queries. This refinement brings queries closer to the surface and encourages rays from different views to access features near the same location. The ablation shows improved intersection and normal accuracy over endpoint-only and uniform sampling.

The same structure enables us to amortize representation construction across objects. We build a feedforward 3D U-Net on octree-based CNNs [(Wang et al., 2017)] to predict voxel-corner features from colored point clouds. Averaging predictions at shared vertices produces a consistent feature field, which is decoded by the shared intersection MLP. Training the feature extractor and decoder jointly with rendering losses allows a single checkpoint to construct geometry and appearance for new inputs without per-object optimization. NeuOctree thus supports both per-object compression and feedforward construction within the same representation and renderer.

We evaluate per-object compression on seven meshes from Thingi10K and the Stanford 3D Scanning Repository at four storage budgets. NeuOctree achieves the lowest positional error in 24 of 28 model–budget comparisons and competitive normal accuracy compared with geometry-only methods, and significantly overperforms N-BVH and VQAD which jointly represent geometry and appearance. On the separate feedforward task, a shared checkpoint constructs a representation in 0.05 seconds with lower intersection error, compared with approximately 3.5 minutes for N-BVH fitting under the reported settings. The same checkpoint, trained on Objaverse, transfers to ShapeNet without retraining. We further demonstrate direct ray-traced rendering with reshading, reflection, refraction, and fisheye projection, and show image-conditioned generation of NeuOctree assets as a downstream application. Our contributions are:

  • -

    A structured neural surface representation that jointly encodes geometry and appearance in shared voxel-corner features and supports direct ray-traced rendering.

  • -

    Recurrent intersection refinement that adaptively queries the continuous feature field to improve the accuracy of predicted surface intersections and normals.

  • -

    Feedforward representation construction that predicts renderable NeuOctree assets without per-object optimization, with demonstrated transfer across datasets and native 3D generation as a downstream application.

    • 2 Related Work

    Neural Surface and Radiance Representations.

    Neural implicit fields provide a compact and differentiable alternative to explicit geometry. Early methods represented shapes with coordinate-based multilayer perceptrons, using signed distance functions (SDFs) [(Park et al., 2019; Chabra et al., 2020)] or occupancy fields [(Mescheder et al., 2019)]. Subsequent approaches introduced octrees and adaptive spatial partitions [(Takikawa et al., 2021; Martel et al., 2021)], while neural radiance fields jointly modeled density and appearance through volume rendering [(Mildenhall et al., 2020)]. Octree and hash-grid variants [(Yu et al., 2021; Fridovich-Keil et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020b; Müller et al., 2022)], SDF–density hybrids [(Wang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023)], and explicit rasterization-based representations [(Huang et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025)] have substantially improved memory use or image-rendering speed.

    These methods nevertheless expose a mismatch with surface ray tracing. A density or occupancy value does not directly specify a ray–surface intersection, normal, or material; obtaining these quantities typically requires repeated field evaluations, surface localization, or mesh extraction. The resulting geometric ambiguity can compromise fine detail, and level-set formulations often rely on an inside–outside convention that is awkward for open or non-watertight surfaces. NeuOctree instead makes the ray–surface query the representation’s primary interface: a shared decoder predicts the hit, position, normal, and albedo from a ray and a continuous octree feature field. This design preserves the compactness of neural representations while enabling direct ray-traced rendering without an intermediate mesh or texture-baking stage.

    Neural Mesh Compression.

    Traditional mesh compression combines connectivity coding, coordinate quantization, and simplification to reduce storage while preserving surface fidelity [(Deering, 1995; Chow, 1997; Diaz-Gutierrez et al., 2005; Touma & Gotsman, 1998; Heckbert & Garland, 1999)]. Learning-based methods replace hand-designed operators with graph networks or lightweight MLPs that upsample a coarse mesh and predict vertex displacements [(Liu et al., 2020a; Chen et al., 2023; Sivaram et al., 2024; Pentapati et al., 2025)]. Although effective for individual assets, these approaches are generally optimized per mesh, focus primarily on geometry, and require a fixed coarse topology; appearance is commonly handled by a separate texture-baking step. N-BVH [(Weier et al., 2024)] is closer to our setting because it predicts ray intersections and appearance within a hierarchical structure, but it also relies on object-specific optimization.

    NeuOctree addresses these limitations with a sparse octree that supplies a global spatial prior and shared voxel-corner features that provide local context. Geometry and appearance are decoded through the same ray-query interface, so the representation can be optimized as a compact per-object asset or predicted by a shared network across objects. The distinction is therefore not only a different compression structure, but also a shift from per-mesh fitting to a renderable representation that supports feedforward construction.

    Structured 3D Learning and Feedforward Reconstruction.

    Point-, voxel-, and sparse-voxel networks have become standard tools for 3D perception and generation [(Qi et al., 2017a; Qi et al., 2017b; Li et al., 2018; Maturana & Scherer, 2015; Wu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017; Graham et al., 2018; Choy et al., 2019; Wang, 2023; Wu et al., 2024)]. Their structured spatial domains support scalable feature extraction, but their outputs are typically occupancies, semantic features, or task-specific predictions rather than a representation that can be queried directly by a surface renderer. NeuOctree uses the same structured prior for a different purpose: an octree U-Net predicts features at voxel corners from colored point clouds, and averaging shared vertices yields a consistent continuous field for the ray-intersection decoder. This establishes a direct bridge between feedforward 3D learning and surface rendering: one shared checkpoint constructs geometry and appearance without per-object optimization, while the resulting representation remains suitable for ray tracing and can serve as a native output space for 3D generation.

    3 Method

    Overview.

    NeuOctree is built around a direct surface query. An asset is represented by an occupied sparse octree and a continuous feature field defined on its voxel corners. Given a ray segment inside an occupied voxel, a shared decoder predicts whether the ray hits the surface and, if so, the intersection position, normal, and albedo. The same decoder is used for every voxel and every ray; only the octree topology and its feature values vary across assets. This separation lets us use the representation in two regimes: a feature table can be optimized for one asset, or an octree network can predict the feature field in a single feedforward pass. In both cases the output is directly consumable by a surface ray tracer and does not require mesh extraction or texture baking.

    3.1 Structured Neural Surface Representation

    Sparse octree and continuous feature field.

    We construct an octree from the input point cloud and retain its occupied leaf voxels. The octree provides a structured support for spatial queries and lets the renderer skip empty space. For an occupied voxel v, let {f_v,ijk}_i,j,k∈{0,1} denote its eight corner features. At a local coordinate q∈[0,1]³, the decoder reads the continuous feature field by trilinear interpolation,

    φᵥ(q)=∑_i,j,k∈{0,1}wᵢⱼₖ(q) f_v,ijk,

    where wᵢⱼₖ are the standard trilinear weights. Corner features shared by adjacent voxels are identified as one vertex feature, so interpolation remains continuous across voxel boundaries. In per-object optimization, the unique vertex features are learned directly. In the feedforward model, the network first predicts eight corner slots for each occupied voxel; slots that refer to the same geometric vertex are averaged before rendering. This deterministic aggregation converts voxel outputs into the same shared feature field used by the optimized representation.

    For the colored feedforward setting, the interpolated field can be augmented with a voxel-local residual feature. We optionally use a pooled input-color prior in the material branch. These terms provide local appearance context without changing the surface-query interface or shared vertex field.

    Ray-query decoder.

    For a ray traversing voxel v, we denote the local entry and exit points by pᵢₙ and pₒᵤₜ, and use d=norm(pₒᵤₜ-pᵢₙ) as the local ray direction. At a query position q, a geometry branch receives the interpolated feature, the local position, the ray direction, and the current refinement state. A separate material branch uses the same spatial feature field and ray information together with the current position and color state. Both branches are lightweight residual MLPs whose weights are shared across all voxels and rays. Their outputs are

    (a,z,sₕ)=G_θ(φᵥ(q),q,d,state), c=σ (M_θ(φᵥ(q),q,d,state)),

    where a∈ℝ³ parameterizes the position, z∈ℝ³ is normalized to produce the surface normal, sₕ is the hit logit, and σ is the sigmoid function. The predicted hit probability is h=σ(sₕ) and the predicted albedo is c∈[0,1]³.

    The position parameterization is ray-local. In the segment-bounded variant used by the feedforward rendering configuration, the first component of σ(a) gives α∈[0,1] and

    p̂=pᵢₙ+α(pₒᵤₜ-pᵢₙ).

    The per-object geometry compression protocol uses the equivalent ray-projection parameterization, which projects the predicted local point onto the current ray line. When the segment-bounded option is enabled, this projection is restricted to the current segment. Both forms preserve the key property that the decoder predicts a surface intersection rather than a density level set. Fourier position features are not used in the reported configurations.

    3.2 Recurrent Intersection Refinement

    Samples taken only at a voxel boundary can be far from the surface, and the boundary point depends on viewing direction even when rays observe the same surface point. A single boundary query therefore makes the decoder learn an unnecessarily view-dependent mapping. We use the predicted intersection to place later queries in the continuous feature field.

    Let qₖ be the k-th adaptive query. The decoder produces an intersection estimate p̂ₖ and the next query is obtained by projecting this estimate back onto the current ray parameterization,

    qₖ₊₁=Π_ray(p̂ₖ),

    where Π_ray denotes ray-line projection or its segment-bounded variant, depending on the chosen position parameterization. The recurrent decoder can maintain a chained hidden state across iterations. Our pooled variant, used for the reported compression and sampling experiments, encodes the entry and exit points as ordinary members of the feature set, initializes the first interior query at the segment midpoint, and then adds further adaptively placed queries from the preceding readout. The per-query hidden increments are averaged before a shared output head predicts the final attributes. With three adaptive iterations this gives five feature reads per voxel segment (entry, exit, and three adaptive queries). The fixed-sampling ablations use the same decoder modules and replace only the adaptive positions with predetermined positions.

    This construction couples all queries to the same local feature field while moving later queries toward the surface. It therefore improves localization and normal prediction without introducing a large per-voxel network or requiring volume samples along the entire ray. When the chained recurrent variant is used, intermediate predictions are also supervised; at inference we use the final stage.

    3.3 Octree Traversal and Surface Rendering

    Given a camera ray, we enumerate its intersections with occupied leaf voxels in front-to-back order. Each candidate is represented by its local entry and exit points and the index of its voxel feature block. The decoder is evaluated on these candidates in chunks. A candidate is accepted when its hit probability exceeds a threshold; the first accepted candidate for each ray is selected. Its local position is converted back to octree coordinates by adding the voxel origin, while the predicted normal and albedo are retained as surface attributes. Rays for which no candidate is accepted return the background value. Thus octree traversal replaces the broad volume sampling used by neural radiance fields, and the selected attributes can be passed directly to a standard ray-tracing integrator for reshading, reflection, refraction, or other camera effects.

    3.4 Feedforward Representation Construction

    The structured representation makes feature construction amortizable across objects. We build an input octree from a colored point cloud and attach point color, local point offset, and normalized global coordinates to occupied cells. An octree-based U-Net [(Wang et al., 2017)] processes this sparse hierarchy with octree convolutions, downsampling and upsampling stages, residual blocks, and skip connections. At the query depth, it predicts a tensor with eight feature slots per occupied voxel. Reshaping these slots and averaging all slots that share a geometric vertex yields the continuous field used by the decoder.

    The feature extractor and the ray-query decoder are trained jointly with the same rendering losses used for per-object optimization. Consequently, a single checkpoint maps a new colored point cloud to a renderable NeuOctree without optimizing the object-specific feature table. The resulting field is also a native output space for the image-conditioned generation pipeline in Section 4.3.

    3.5 Training Objective

    Training supervision is obtained by unprojecting RGB–D images into camera rays. For every occupied ray–voxel segment before the ground-truth surface, we store a hit label, the local intersection position, the oriented normal, and the albedo. Let m denote the hit label and let ℙ be the positive surface pairs. The pointwise objective is

    L_PNCH=Lₚ(ℙ)+Lₙ(ℙ)+λₕLₕᵢₜ(h,m)+λ_cL_color(c,c^*;ℙ),

    where Lₚ and Lₙ are position and normal reconstruction losses, Lₕᵢₜ is BCE (or its class-balanced variant), and L_color is a relative color reconstruction loss. The geometry terms are masked by the ground-truth hit labels; in the feedforward configuration their normalization is restricted to positive surface pairs so that empty ray–voxel segments do not dilute the surface signal.

    For colored reconstruction, we supplement the pointwise terms with image-level normal and albedo SSIM losses, together with optional smoothness, color constancy, detail-gradient, and hit-topology regularizers. In compact form,

    L=∑ₖwₖ(L_PNCH⁽ᵏ⁾+λ_imgL_img⁽ᵏ⁾+λₜₒₚₒLₜₒₚₒ⁽ᵏ⁾), ∑ₖwₖ=1,

    where k indexes recurrent stages. Image terms are masked by valid surface pixels when configured, while hit-topology terms penalize holes, floaters, and boundary inconsistencies. Geometry-only experiments use the corresponding subset to supervise the renderer.

    4 Results

    4.1 Results of Per-Mesh Compression

    We compare NeuOctree with the per-object optimization methods NGF [(Sivaram et al., 2024)], QNDF [(Pentapati et al., 2025)], VQAD [(Takikawa et al., 2022)], and N-BVH [(Weier et al., 2024)] over a broad range of storage budgets. VQAD is adapted to predict surface normals and intersection positions under the same geometry supervision.

    Dataset and Metrics.

    We evaluate the seven meshes in Table1 from the Stanford 3D Scanning Repository [(Stanford University, 1994)] and Thingi10K [(Zhou & Jacobson, 2016)], rendering 16 fixed 512×512 views. We report mean ray–surface position error dₚₘ in normalized object coordinates, scaled by 10³, and oriented normal error dₙₒᵣₘ in degrees.

    Geometry Compression.

    As shown in Table1, NeuOctree obtains the lowest dₚₘ in 24 of 28 model–budget comparisons. It wins all 21 at 81–244 KiB and three of seven at 823 KiB, where QNDF takes the other four. NeuOctree also wins 12 normal-error comparisons; NGF leads mainly at the smallest payload, while QNDF is competitive only at the largest. Thus, the strongest baseline changes with payload, whereas NeuOctree maintains the most consistent positional accuracy. The curves in Fig.4 and qualitative results in Fig.3 corroborate this trend, showing cleaner silhouettes and better preservation of fine structures.

    Joint Geometry and Appearance Compression.

    On Objaverse, per-object NeuOctree achieves the best normal accuracy and PSNR; on ShapeNet, it is best on all three metrics in Table3. Relative to VQAD, it reduces dₚₘ and dₙₒᵣₘ by 85.5% and 37.8% on Objaverse while adding 1.11 dB PSNR. The ShapeNet improvements are 95.8%, 32.6%, and 9.33 dB, respectively. Representative albedo reconstructions are shown in Fig.5.

    Sampling Strategy Ablation.

    We compare recurrent sampling with endpoint-only and four-sample uniform variants. Recurrent sampling reduces dₚₘ and dₙₒᵣₘ by 7.7% and 9.4% relative to uniform sampling, and by 12.0% and 17.0% relative to endpoint-only sampling. This supports querying the feature field near the predicted surface rather than at fixed locations.

    Open-Surface Reconstruction.

    We evaluate NeuOctree and VQAD on an open glass pane using an 823 KiB budget. For matched mirrored face-on cameras, we back-project both depth maps and measure their separation dz along the pane normal at pixels visible from both sides (Fig.6). NeuOctree matches the GT median dz=0, whereas VQAD gives dz=0.059 world units, revealing a systematic two-sided offset. These results support NeuOctree’s ability to represent open surfaces without an inside–outside labeling like VQAD.

    4.2 Results of Feedforward Methods

    Dataset and Metrics.
