A user can trade-off the limited predictive capability of the MLP parameter model with the reliability of nearest neighbours, according to the intended application.

    VI Evaluation

    VI-ASelf-Consistency Check

    Prior to the qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we perform a sanity-check experiment to verify the robustness of the learned embedding space. More specifically, we assess whether sampling latent vectors according to the learned MoG distribution, decoding them into trajectory space, and subsequently re-projecting the generated trajectories back into the latent space through the encoder, results in latent points that still adhere to the learned MoG distribution (Figure 15). For sampling, we use 2k points to match the size of the training dataset. From Figure 15, we confirm both visually and quantitatively, through the obtained metric value of .705 (<1), that the learned latent space is self-consistent.

    VI-BAssessment Premise

    Our aim in this evaluation is to investigate two claims, (i) that following the guidance of our learned latent distribution gives an advantage over no guidance for generation, and (ii) our model encodes information tailored to the real data. Hence, in order to determine the evaluation framework, we discuss each claim and reach a comparison objective that will provide evidence for our claims.

    For (i), we use an existing set of trajectories, tₕ, say from simulator, h. We compute z_R,zₕ via z=E_θ(τ), and sample ℤ to get z_G, where the distribution of our posterior (G) is closer to the real latents than the distribution of zₕ (e.g., just the sampled prior). Then we use the trained decoder D_θ:ℤ→T to get decoded τ_G,S, where τ_S the decoded version of τₕ. Finally we compare τ_G and τ_S, aiming to prove that the trajectories with latents more faithful to the distribution of z_R, are closer to the real trajectories, than the other latents. We use both CCP baseline and the prior as the sampled distributions, and so, we compare the generated trajectories from our posterior, the prior, and the CCP empirical distribution.

    For (ii), let there be E^′ an alternative encoder, e.g., MPACT, then, p_R=E^′(τ_R). We sample from the distribution of p_R to get p_G. We obtain τ^′_G via a known decoder D^′. We compare our obtained τ_G and τ^′_G to the real data. In practice this essentially means comparing the trajectories decoded from two latent distributions: our inferred MoG (τ_G), and the distribution of the observed embeddings of another parameter space, MPACT (τ^′_G).

    Thus, we compare our posterior with MPACT (ii), prior and other simulators (i). We emphasise that all comparisons are made between trajectories generated through our decoder, to ensure that we do not inherently compare simulator specifics, but the embeddings of these simulated data against the real.

    VI-CQuantitative Assessment

    In order to quantify “closeness” to the real data, we sample the latent distributions of five sources, i.e., prior, inferred MoG, RVO, CCP baseline, and MPACT. We compute three types of metrics on trajectories from our decoder for comparison fairness; we want to exclude accumulated limitations of different simulators. So, for each source, we sample their distributions to obtain a set of trajectories and compare them with the real ground truths. Specifically, we calculate: (a) our latent metric described in Section IV-C, (b) the Maximum Mean Discrepancy-MMD [49] values (statistical measure for comparing distributions), (c) Sliced Wasserstein Distance [50] (SWD), and (d) the energy distance of each set of generated data against the real data. We use SWD because we do not have 1-1 matching of trajectories and want to measure them containing similar behaviours. SWD measures the similarity between two distributions by comparing their projections along multiple random 1D directions and averaging the resulting Wasserstein distances. The energy distance is a direct distributional distance between two unpaired sets, like MMD, but does not require choosing a kernel. We finally calculate (e) the Jensen-Shannon Divergence-JSD (symmetric and stable measure for comparing probability distributions): for trajectory features (x/z positions and speeds) and other additional trajectory-based behaviour measures (Deviation From Goal-DFG and Movement Direction Diversity-MDD). We report these values in Table IV.

    From Table IV we can see that the MoG distribution is closest to the real data in the majority of the metrics, outperforming the prior and MPACT, and so providing evidence for our claims (i) and (ii). Additionally, MPACT achieves overall better scores among the simulator sources, with RVO being second best. We can also see that our metric follows the emergent “trends” of the other established metrics, i.e, the ranking of the “best” sources is consistent. The energy distance ranks CCP second best, which again reveals that different metrics focus on different aspects. Hence, some discrepancies between metrics appear, which is sensible since different metrics often assess different aspects of behaviours/simulations. Therefore, the goal is not to replace existing metrics, but to introduce an additional measure that captures complementary aspects of behavioural similarity.

    Further contextualising the results, Table V reports an extra set of metrics that operate on the latent space (apart from our latent metric): latent energy, and MoG Wasserstein Distance. Fréchet Distance [51] measures the similarity between two trajectories by quantifying the minimum maximum distance required to traverse both paths while preserving their point ordering. We refrain from using Fréchet Distance on the trajectory space since it becomes extremely slow, and instead, we calculate it on the “core” trajectories found from each inference run, and report the ranking in decreasing order: MPACT, RVO, and CCP. Latent energy and MoG WD ranking coincide with that of the latent metric. Overall, the ranking trends provide additional evidence for the quantitative evaluation.

    VI-DQualitative Assessment

    Next, we visualise some of the aforementioned results, for qualitative inspection. Figure 17 shows the heatmaps illustrating the difference in the correlation matrices of real and generated data, for four sets of generated data, each associated with a different empirical latent distribution. Correlation matrices [52] are built by computing trajectory features, i.e., positions x and z, speed, acceleration and angular difference, to find whether correlations and dependencies between features are preserved. Taking the difference from the real data matrix, assess representativeness to the real data features. We observe that our posterior returns the smallest differences with MPACT being a close second. Finally, we plot boxplots of the trajectory features (positions and speed) of the real data, and the four sources (excluding the prior) in Figure 16, showing that our MoG posterior and the MPACT generations are closer to the real data, confirming the quantitative assessment observations.

    VII Discussion

    In this work, we learn an encoding that yields a latent representation, embedding real data features, thus parameterising trajectory information. To do this, we utilised trajectories captured in real life to train a VAE on the task of trajectory reconstruction. We use the trained model encoder to build a posterior distribution (MoG) based on the observed data (latents of the real data), according to predicted cluster centres (k-means clustering). Then we employ our method for embedding synthetic data from various simulators to measure latent distribution similarity. The feature space is aligned with the real one, enabling comparisons between the two sets of latent distributions. We can then inform the selection of latents, and guide it towards a distribution of choice. This functionality enables measuring behaviour fidelity in an aligned embedding space which is useful for comparing synthetic data to real, as well as for assessing whether new training datasets contain behavioural features that adhere to those of the real ones.

    Limitations and Future Work

    Despite the new opportunities that our method offers, it has some limitations. Our model does not take into account environmental information explicitly, e.g., POIs, in its inputs, which limits our system’s ability to assign specific semantic meaning to the latent space, e.g., action labels. Also, it does not directly receive information regarding neighbouring actions and group behaviours. But, these actions are implicitly entangled into the input trajectories, since it falls upon the simulator to produce paths that mimic the real ones, including the spawns and densities of agents. Still, it would be beneficial to further experiment with such aspects in the input representation which, however, would require more data since the task becomes more difficult.

    Additionally, the amount of real data is limited and so the model cannot capture the full range of behavioural features that could emerge. The absence of a large corpus of tracked trajectories captured in-the-wild affects both the encoding power and choice of architecture. Experimenting with more advanced model architectures, e.g., transformers, would be interesting, which entails the creation of a larger training database of real trajectories. Finally, our method is not extensively assessed against a large variety of alternative quantitative and qualitative metrics, an analysis that would reveal both its strengths and weaknesses. However, the lack of baseline state-of-the-art scores, benchmark evaluation metrics and tasks, makes the proper formulation of such a protocol an interesting but challenging direction for future work.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：人群模拟器的能力高度依赖训练数据的类型与多样性，而现有泛化指标几乎测不出这点。

要点：

  • 目标：让 crowd simulation 生成的 agent 行为更丰富、自然，并贴合所处环境；近年用机器学习直接从轨迹数据学出行为模式，能捕捉越来越复杂的人群动力学
  • 但作者指出，这些系统的能力**强烈依赖训练数据的类型与多样性**——换个场地、换个密度分布就可能失效
  • 文章主张把「数据」本身嵌成表示（Trajeform），并指出多数现有指标在评估「模拟器泛化到真实数据集」时存在明显缺陷，需要更合适的衡量方式

为什么值得看：人群/交通这类模拟在引擎里常被当作「参数调一调就行」，实际瓶颈是训练数据覆盖不到的场景。把数据表示与泛化度量一起摆上台面，比再加一个损失项更有价值——尤其对做开放世界人流、活动疏散的团队。

中文摘要：人群模拟的目标是生成丰富、自然且与环境相称的 agent 行为。近年来机器学习让这类行为可以直接从轨迹数据中学到，模型因此能捕捉越来越复杂的人群动力学；但作者指出，这些系统的能力强烈依赖训练时所用数据的类型与多样性，一旦面对分布不同的真实数据集就未必成立。文章提出 Trajeform，把人群数据本身嵌入成一种表示，并讨论如何更合理地评估「模拟器对真实世界数据集的泛化」——因为现有的大多数指标在这一维度上存在明显局限。对把人群模拟当作管线一环的引擎团队，这篇提醒的是：先看数据覆盖，再谈模型能力。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-11-02

Trajeform: Embedding Crowd Data

Abstract

Crowd simulation aims to generate agent behaviours that are rich, natural, and appropriate to their surrounding environment. Recent advances in Machine Learning have enabled such behavioural patterns to be learned directly from trajectory data, allowing simulation models to capture increasingly complex crowd dynamics. However, the capabilities of these systems remain strongly dependent on the type and diversity of the data used during training. When evaluating how well crowd simulators generalise to real-world datasets, most existing metrics focus primarily on trajectory-level differences rather than behaviour-level similarity. In this paper, we present Trajeform, a framework that trains a reconstruction VAE (Variational Autoencoder) on real trajectory data to learn a meaningful continuous embedding that preserves behavioural characteristics of real crowds. The trained encoder can then be applied to synthetic trajectories generated by simulators and used to compare the resulting embedding distributions. Additionally, the learned embedding can be used to analyse supplementary data, such as trajectories corresponding to a simulator’s principal behaviours or captured data from controlled environments (e.g., cycling), providing insight into their ability to span the real behavioural embedding space. The framework compares data from three simulators (CCP, modCCP, and RVO) against ground-truth datasets and is evaluated quantitatively and qualitatively using latent-space analysis, distributional metrics, and trajectory generation through sampling from the aggregated posterior distribution. The results indicate that the learned latent space captures meaningful trajectory dependencies found in the real data, making the framework useful both as an additional measure of synthetic data believability and as a tool for informing the training of future trajectory models.

I Introduction

Crowd simulation aims to populate virtual environments with realistic agent movements. Within this scope, the umbrella of realism includes behaviour diversity, richness, and contextual awareness, in that agents should not only move naturally, but also behave in ways that are appropriate to the environment, e.g., a university campus. Extensive research has achieved advanced simulators for generating believable agents [1, 2, 3], utilised in crowd authoring to optimise simulator parameter spaces with respect to an authoring constraint [4, 5]. However, most of these systems either rely on manual parameterisation [1], or synthetic data [4]. Works that utilise real data are often constrained by the amount and type of data they use (single policy [6], controlled environments [7, 8]), hence hindering generalisability. Therefore, it is imperative to measure behavioural similarity by comparing differently sourced agent behaviours with real data [9]. In this work, we aim to quantify and formalise an embedding representation to assess the quality of agent behaviours in comparison with real ones. Such a tool enables comparing real and simulated behaviours in the representation space, and informing a selection of parameters spanning the real data features.

Measuring behaviour similarity properly, in the context of crowds, is a challenging undertaking due to the conceptual definition of a behaviour “match” and its non-deterministic nature. Relevant works weigh hand-crafted salient features [10, 5], perceptually validate realism [11, 12], or combine both (perceptually-validated metric) [13]. However, these works still focus on trajectory faithfulness, and are biased either on the selection of trajectory features, or the expertise of user study participants. Other works utilise entropy-based measures [14, 15]. To compare simulated and real data, several systems [16, 4] report metrics on trajectory features such as Deviation From Goal (DFG), and Optimal Path (OP) [17]. Even though these metrics are widely used and can give strong indications regarding the distribution of trajectory features in the two groups (generated and real), they are more tailored to trajectory features in an aggregated manner (e.g., DFG for all agents at every timestep); these partially capture behavioural aspects (turning left and turning right contain the same behaviour but lead to different paths) or limit controllability. We aim to investigate learnable features to complement the assembly of metrics used for comparing between two sets of behaviours.

In this paper, we introduce Trajeform, a trajectory-based framework that learns an embedding space directly from real crowd trajectory data. The learned latent distribution serves as a baseline, against which synthetic trajectories (e.g., generated by crowd simulators) can be compared. Synthetic trajectories are projected onto the learned latent space, allowing their inferred distributions to be juxtaposed with the real-data embedding distribution. The framework preserves the properties of a VAE latent space while encouraging behaviourally similar trajectories to cluster together. Since the model is trained through trajectory reconstruction, the decoder can additionally be used to project latent embeddings back into the trajectory space. Trajeform primarily aims to project crowd data onto an embedding space tailored to real behavioural features. To achieve this, the framework operates on canonicalised trajectories aligned during preprocessing, encouraging the model to focus on behavioural characteristics beyond simple positional attributes such as spawn location or orientation. Consequently, the learned embedding space captures more behaviour-relevant representations. Beyond measuring behaviour similarity, the framework can also provide indications regarding how effectively a simulator spans the real-data behavioural manifold, while additionally informing simulator parameter selections towards distributions more consistent with the arrangement of real data in the latent space. We evaluate the proposed framework through comparisons with established quantitative metrics, complemented by graphical analyses of the learned embedding distributions.

In a nutshell, we deliver a model trained on real data, that transforms trajectories to learned latent features. The trained latents compile a distribution used as a baseline for comparisons with differently-sourced data, e.g., simulated. Hence, our contribution can be summarised as follows:

  • •

    Learning to embed crowd data in a feature space aligned with real behavioural characteristics, and

  • •

    Inferring a latent distribution from real data embeddings, enabling informed sampling, and similarity measurement in latent space.

    • II Related Work

    II-ATrajectory-based Metrics

    To compare simulations—either with synthetic or real data—various quantitative metrics have been proposed. At the macroscopic level, the Fundamental Diagram [18] is widely used, relating speed, density, and flow to capture global crowd phenomena. At the microscopic level, metrics focus on per-trajectory features such as deviation from goals, path optimality, and distance to nearest neighbours, which can indicate behaviours like grouping. Another approach compares distributions of trajectory features, such as speed and position. Several crowd simulators leverage fundamental diagrams and low-level features for validation [16, 1, 6]. However, such metrics are more tailored to trajectory replication instead of behaviour similarity and so they are often sensitive to outliers or detailed motions [19, 20]. Some works benchmark evaluations, but specifically for steering behaviours [21]. Charalambous et al. [22] propose a method for outlier detection through a data-driven approach, while Lerner et al. [23] perform database matching. More recently, Wang et al. [9] employ Bayesian inference to discover latent path patterns from trajectory data for the analysis and comparison of crowd behaviours. Our method is complementary to other techniques, and does not perform inference on the trajectory space, but on a compressed latent representation using an end-to-end architecture.

    Perhaps closer to our method is Crowd Space [15] that defines agent descriptors (Minimal Predicted Distance) and trains a dimensionality reduction model to find the most suitable simulator for a given real scenario. This method learns a manifold based on the proposed agent-centric entropy [15, 14]. In our method however, we do not specify the evaluation metric, but instead, allow the model to learn features freely, and derive a metric post-training, using our learned manifold. Also, we employ a variational model, improving the sampling and generative capabilities. Crowd Space aims to assess the predictive accuracy of simulators to find the best simulation method to use on new crowd scenarios. Our method focuses on learning meaningful embeddings from real data, emphasising representation rather than classification. Crowd Space in trained on a larger set of real data that includes controlled and dense environments [7, 24], whereas we aim at in-the-wild behaviours. Finally, in Trajeform, we do not group our trajectories according to their scenario source, e.g., University Campus, but rather, learn a collective representation since behaviours in two different scenarios could be the same.

    II-BPerceptual Evaluation

    Apart from using quantitative methods to evaluate trajectory and behaviour plausibility, perceptual evaluation is also explored as a way to mitigate for the aforementioned metric limitations. User studies have been implemented to assess trajectory realism [25, 26, 27, 28]. O’Connor et al. [29] conduct a study to determine whether users find crowd behaviours to be more realistic with a Social Force model, and its implications in psychophysical experimentation. Smaller user studies have also been conducted as part of a larger evaluation protocol of proposed optimisation models [4], or authoring tools [30] asking users to report on believability and usability. Still, user studies, especially in the domain of virtual crowds, are highly dependent on the study design, the experience of participants in the domain, and general visualisation aspect of the shown stimuli, e.g., body animation, clothing, facial animation, and environment quality [31, 32]. Daniel et al. [13] propose a quality metric that combines comparison metrics with perceptual tools. Although existing quantitative and qualitative evaluation approaches have been proven useful in uncovering certain behavioural aspects of simulated agents, in our method we compare directly with real data, using learned features and so alleviating the need to hand-craft quantitative metrics but also avoid the perceptual biases. Our method can be used as an additional approach, complementary to other metrics.

    II-CTrajectory Representation

    Representing trajectories and trajectory-based behaviours is also important for analysis and comparisons. Morphable Crowds by Ju et al. [7] employs a data-driven method to build a trajectory model and create behaviour prefabs, while GREIL by Charalambous et al. [6] learns an inverse Reinforcement Learning policy from real data. Pure trajectory information usually has higher dimensionality p=(t,x,z)∈(T,2) and contains low-interpretability features in terms of behavioural characteristics, e.g., assigning behaviour labels to a distribution of positional data is not straightforward. Therefore, multiple works have attempted to transform pure trajectories to some compressed representations, e.g., trajectory images [4, 33], trajectory parameters [5]. Additional works employ learning-based methods to encode trajectory information into high-level parameters, e.g., combination of common behaviours [1], and OCEAN personality attributes [34]. High-level trajectory embeddings enhance explainability and assist comparison and analysis, however, the extracted features are dependent on the data used, which is often not sourced from real scenarios. Conversely, approaches based on real data, lack controllability and generalisability [35], especially if said data come from controlled settings instead of in-the-wild. Here, we strive for an embedding based on real, in-the-wild data, employing a learning-based method to allow the model freedom to learn appropriate behavioural and trajectory features that would be challenging to define through traditional feature specification.

    II-DCrowd Data

    Having crowd data is essential for improving simulation systems, as it supports data-driven methods [23] and provides training data for ML models. While both synthetic and real data can be used, real datasets are preferable because they capture complex, hard-to-replicate crowd dynamics. Such data can be used for training (if sufficiently large) or for evaluating new simulators [36, 15]. Crowd data typically consists of agent trajectories, including at least 2D positions and often orientations. Ideally, datasets would be paired, containing ground truth annotations (e.g., behavioural descriptions), which are crucial for supervised learning. However, collecting such data is challenging. Trajectories are usually obtained either through video tracking or motion capture, with data gathered in controlled settings [7, 8] or in real environments ranging from sparse to dense crowds [24, 37]. Due to the difficulty of large-scale motion capture, most datasets rely on video-based tracking. Widely used datasets include those from [38, 39], covering environments such as a church yard, a shopping street, and a university campus, as well as video-based datasets like [40]. Despite these efforts, there remains a lack of large paired datasets, limiting the ability of learning-based approaches to extract behaviour patterns. As a result, many works rely on synthetic data tailored to their specific needs.

    III Overview

    III-AProblem Definition

    First, let us define some notations. Let T⊆ℝ²ˣᵀ be the trajectory space, where T is the maximum trajectory length, associated with path duration which is measured in number of frames - directly corresponding to duration (s) since timestep is kept fixed. Also in the trajectory space, let τᵗ be the 2D position at time t, with τ∈T a trajectory point. We define τ_C to be the set of category-specific trajectories, with C={R,S,G} denoting real, synthetic, and generated, respectively.

    Our goal is to train an encoder E_θ:T→ℤ, subject to parameters θ, that creates a mapping from the trajectory space to the latent space ℤ⊆ℝ^Z with latent dimensions Z, where latent point z∈ℤ. Given the trained encoder, real data τ_R and simulated trajectories τ_f,h, we can obtain z_R,z_f and zₕ via zᵢ=E_θ(τᵢ). If there are simulators f:ℙ_f→T and h:ℙₕ→T, where ℙᵢ a simulator-specific parameter space, suppose that f,h attempt to simulate the real data. Then, comparing the distributions of z_f and zₕ against z_R, we can provide an indication of how well they represent the real data distribution. If τ_f,h are two different datasets to be used for training a trajectory model, the latent distribution comparisons help indicate how close the training set would be to the existing real data - a measure analogous to class balancing. We theorise that (i) our latent space meaningfully reflects the structure of real data, and (ii) the properties of our latent space (continuous, meaningful, preserving real behavioural features) make our encoder more tailored to the real data. As part of this work, we provide evidence of these claims via two sets of experiments (Section VI).

    We aim towards a smooth, continuous latent space, that is generative but also has interpretable structure. This latent space, achieved based on the trained encoder E_θ, can be used for:

  • •

    Graphical comparison of simulator data (e.g., CCP) with the real data they attempt to simulate (e.g., commercial street).

  • •

    Distribution comparison between the encoded simulated and real data in the latent space.

  • •

    Graphical observation of the coverage of the embedding space of differently-sourced data (e.g., principal behaviours of CCP, or data from a controlled environment).

  • •

    Selection of training data of simulator-specific parameters.

    • III-BModel

    Our goal is to learn an embedding function subject to trajectory information from real data. Considering the real data size, we incorporate encoder/decoder modules that work well on lower cardinality. Thus, we train a VAE on the task of trajectory reconstruction, and define our learned latent space as the desired manifold. We approach the training setup as follows: (a) we train a VAE on reconstruction without explicitly incorporating a prediction of the generated trajectory length, and (b) learn an additional feed-forward model to predict the path length [lᵢ;i≤Lₘₐₓ], from the latent space ℤ. We do this since our data vary in path durations and so we help our decoder generate more appropriate paths at inference time, by inputting the predicted length in the form of a mask matrix. Hence, the whole model is trained on the loss given in Equation 1, with β=.1. The low value for β comes after experimentation, trading off reconstruction quality and latent space faithfulness to prior distribution ℕ(0,1); other works with related concerns use small KL-divergence weight [41, 42].

    L=L_VAE+L_len.;L_VAE=L_recon.+βL_KL(1)
    L_recon.=MSE(τ)
    L_len.=CrossEntropyon trajectory len. classification

    We experiment with the model architecture, and specifically the architecture for the encoder and decoder blocks. Temporal convolutions are good analysers and could prove useful for feature extraction in our case. At the same time GRUs provide smooth, temporally processed generations. Therefore, we conduct a model tuning study where we experiment with block combinations, as shown in Table I. The table reports the latent losses L_z=||z-z̃||₂ on a common test set. Note that we do not include transformer blocks due to the small training dataset. In the case of a convolutional decoder, the reconstructions return jerky paths due to the block’s focus on preserving local structure, while GRU generators favour smoothness. Since our goal is to create a structured latent space, where similar behaviours in trajectories could be gathered together, we also employed a Mixture of Gaussians as a prior. Ultimately, visualising the quality of the test reconstructions and latent space projections, we proceed with a convolutional (encoder) to GRU (decoder) architecture, denoted conv2gru. Figure 1 illustrates the architecture overview.

    III-CModel Data

    The model has been trained on a set of real data trajectories. In this section, we give details regarding the data processing.

    Real Dataset

    We use existing tracked datasets corresponding to trajectory data captured in a church yard, a university campus, a commercial street, and outside a hotel, henceforth referred to as Flock, Students, Zara, and ETH [39, 38, 40]. The total number of trajectories for each dataset is {24,849,531,750}, respectively, sampled at a timestep =.4, for uniformity. Before continuing to the preprocessing step, we exclude Zara3 from our experiments dataset, and save it for testing. Finally, the datapoints are padded according to the maximum length, and a relevant mask is produced.

    Data Preprocessing

    Prior to training the model, we pass the data through a preprocessing module whose purpose is to canonicalise it in order to help the model learn useful features and not be, for example, biased on the starting position. This module includes: path segmentation, transformations, spatial canonicalisation, and noise addition. More specifically, we disregard paths with LLₘₐₓ=104 to smaller valid parts. The transformations include, translation to the (x,z) origin, rotation of the direction of movement towards the right x-axis, and flipping of x and z-axes to the first quadrant. For spatial canonicalisation, we try both bounding the (x,z) space, and normalising according to (z-zₘₑₐₙ)/z_std. Finally, for noise augmentation we randomly add noise ε sampled from a standard normal. The choice for Lₘₐₓ is justified by the boxplot in Figure 2 which omits the outlier lengths for each dataset. It also shows an example preprocessing module that includes segmentation and transformation as mentioned. For a more detailed visualisation of the preprocessing components, the reader is referred to the supplementary material.

    We ablate the individual components of the preprocessing module. The ablation experiments were conducted with the same underlying model architecture and hyperparameters, for fairness. We do not report on the model losses because the scale is not comparable, e.g., in normalisation, lower losses do not imply better model, or without translation, the model achieves better performance because it learns to reconstruct not according to the trajectory/behaviour features but according to spawn. The final module includes the segmentation and transformation operations, and thus is used in the inference pipeline; note that padding and translation to origin are mandatory. The final training set consists of ~2k samples, and maxLen of 104 frames.

    III-DEmbeddings Visualisation

    After training the VAE model, we visualise some feature maps, as presented in Figure 3. From the figure, we can see that two different trajectory points produce heatmaps of the same convolutional feature that have the same overall structure but differ in the temporal “activation”. On second inspection, these activation frames correspond to the number of unpadded frames in the respective samples, indicating that this feature learns the path length. In Figure 3-right, we can see the heatmap visualisation of the latent layer, revealing the usage of latent dimensions for representation.

    Implementation Details

    Models have been trained using an 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-11800H @ 2.30GHz, 2304 Mhz, 8 Core(s), 16 Logical Processor(s) CPU, 16GBs of RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 GPU. Training took approximately 1.5hours, for 200 epochs (100 the VAE, and 100 the length prediction layer), a batch size of 16, dropout of .2, and 8 latent dimensions, with Adam optimizer and learning rate of 3e⁻⁴.

    IV Results

    At inference time, we utilise the trained model to cluster the real latents, and build a MoG distribution according to the cluster centres and densities. We use this posterior to: test on our control data (Zara3), infer principal trajectories from the posterior means, and sample the distribution to generate informed paths, hence crafting a latent similarity metric between inference and training points.

    IV-APreliminary Results

    Firstly, we take the test dataset we had set aside (Zara3), pass it through the preprocessing block and apply the trained model. The results yield a test reconstruction loss of .959 and a length loss of 3.634. The latent representation of the test trajectories overlay the training latents in Figure 4; the red latent’s sample trajectories are also shown in the bottom left (original and reconstructed). The 8-dimensional latent space was visualised via PCA dimensionality reduction technique [43]. From the visualisation, we can see that the learned latent space encodes the real data in a structured manner, with the test latents fully falling into the trained latent area. We also report the mean latent loss L_z=||z-z̃||₂=.582. This loss was not used during training, but provides an indication of the latent space geometry. More results on the model training can be found in the supplementary material.

    For further testing, we re-train the model on four variants, i.e., holding out each of the four datasets (Flock, ETH, Students, Zara). Then, having these “hold-out models” we test the model by projecting the “unseen” data (e.g., Flock data on the model variant that has been trained on Students-ETH-Zara). Table II documents the mean latent loss; for the latent space projection of the test data, refer to the supplementary material.

    We compare the four test datasets on the full model and on the respective hold-out models. We observe that when leaving out the Flock dataset, the latent loss actually decreases which makes sense since Flock contains few trajectories. We also see that leaving out ETH has the biggest effect on the latent loss hinting that ETH contains behaviours that are rare in the rest of the datasets (this can also be confirmed from the figure that shows a lots of ETH latent points clustering on the top right of the space). This loss difference can also be attributed to the size of the ETH datasets (2nd largest). The average increase of latent loss from the full model to the hold-out variants is from .977 to 1.242, which shows that our model is robust in that it does not just memorise dataset-specific patterns, but rather, unseen real datasets still map coherently into the learned behavioural space. An increase is however expected since the amount of real data is limited (˜2k).

    IV-BLatent Space

    After the preliminary results, we dive deeper into the properties and capabilities of the learned embedding. Firstly, we select families of trajectories in the training data, that we deem “interesting”, and visualise them to inspect for patterns. Figure 5 for example, shows the distribution of speed value in the datasets (left), along with the plotted interesting groups: in this case, the fast and slow trajectories decided via thresholds vₘᵢₙ=.1, and vₘₐₓ=.7. The results show a clear gathering of the two families in opposite ends of the latent space. We confirm this latent property via also inspecting respective results for long-short trajectory pairs, and for agents with high or low variability in their displacements (Δx,Δz) during their paths (the reader is referred to the supplementary material for visualisations).

    VAEs frequently suffer from mode collapse and so to address these concerns, we conduct ablation studies for: training separate spaces per dataset, and comparing against a VQ‑VAE. For the former, Table III reports (for each separately-trained model variant and the full model) the following metrics: the validation reconstruction loss, the number of active dimensions, and the latent entropy. While training the per-dataset variants, we find that the Flock-only variant overfits - which makes sense since the dataset size is considerably limited. Therefore, we exclude it for further observations. Regarding the reconstruction loss, the full model reaches .230 while the average of the three per-dataset variants is .239, showing faithful trajectory representation. Regarding the number of active dimensions (in our 8-dimensional latent space), we find based on the reported values that the latent space is indeed used. Lastly, regarding the normalised latent entropy which we compute to assess whether the latent usage is diverse, Table III shows high values across variants, and so the representation is not concentrated into a few modes. Collectively, these verify that there is no mode collapse. We also train a VQ-VAE variant that essentially replaces the continuous latent variables of a VAE with a finite codebook of learned embeddings, and report a validation reconstruction loss of 1.187 (larger than our VAE). The loss increase along with the our intention to have a continuous space which we can later use for sampling to map back to the trajectory space (through the decoder), provide evidence for the usefulness of the continuous VAE latent space.

    Then, provided a structured and meaningful latent space, we can cluster the embeddings of our training samples, which come from real data. This clustering takes place in the latent space and not in the PCA-projected space. The intuition is that this clustering can be used to build a behaviour distribution tailored to the real data embeddings. We could then use the cluster centres to find the k most common paths, simply by feeding the cluster points into our decoder. Since our model is variational, the latent space is continuous and so this works even if these points do not belong in the original dataset. We use k-means clustering [44] to find the groups. Figure 6 shows such clustering along with the corresponding paths. Given a dataset, this process can be used to obtain the “core behaviours” found within that set. We choose to proceed with k=3 number of latent clusters after both visual observation of the latent space, as well as an ablation analysis (presented and discussed in the supplementary material). As a reminder the generated paths are in canonical form (translated, rotated, and flipped). Variations of these behaviours can be obtained when distributing in the environment by inverting the transformations with randomised parameters; further analysis on intra and inter cluster paths can be found in the supplementary material. In our real data example, we observe that the cluster centres correspond to paths with substantial differences in distance covered, with the shorter core path corresponding to a sparse cluster; this also confirms the findings in Figure 5.

    IV-CGenerations

    Due to the variational component of our model, we can sample the latent space and generate corresponding trajectories. There are three main ways to sample the space: traversing the space, sampling according to the prior (resembles standard normal), or building some posterior distribution. Our aim is to be able to assign meaning to the distribution of the real behaviours in the latent space. Therefore, having the clustering of Section IV-B, we can build a MoG with means equal to the cluster centres and mixture weights proportional to the cluster sizes, i.e., p(z)=π₁ ℕ(z|μ₁,Σ₁)+π₂ ℕ(z|μ₂,Σ₂)+π₃ ℕ(z|μ₃,Σ₃). Supplementary material shows instances of sampling 1k points for each method.

    We can further operate on the latent space by leveraging both the encoder and decoder modules. Specifically, assume that we have a candidate trajectory (e.g., generated by a simulator) that we wish to compare against a real trajectory counterpart. The two trajectories are first projected through the trained encoder onto the latent space, producing zₛ for the unseen latent (synthetic trajectory) and z for the reference latent (real trajectory). Their latent difference can then be computed as:

    ||z-zₛ||₂.

    Since the decoder is trained on real data, we can additionally move from the latent space back to the trajectory space by decoding the reference latent:

    τ̃=D(z),

    and subsequently re-projecting the reconstructed trajectory back into the latent space:

    z̃=E(τ̃).

    Conceptually, the reconstructed latent z̃ should preserve the same behavioural attributes as the original latent z. Therefore, the quantity

    ||z-z̃||₂

    provides an indication of the reconstruction-consistent latent variation that still corresponds to the same underlying behaviour.

    Consequently, the normalised latent metric

    (||z-zₛ||₂)/(||z-z̃||₂)

    can be used as a measure of behavioural similarity between two encoded trajectories, where values <1 indicate a behavioural match.

    Table IV reports this metric for selected examples, which are discussed in more detail in the following sections.

    V Use Cases

    In this section we explore three use cases. Mainly, we compare simulator data that mimic the real, with the ground truths through latent distribution comparisons to reveal behaviour similarity. Then, we test other data sources, e.g., principal simulator behaviours or captured data from controlled environments, to inspect how well the span the latent space, and lastly, use the distribution of the real latents to tune simulator-specific parameters in order to guide simulations towards more “real-data” balanced generations.

    V-ABehaviour Similarity

    We show a use case of our framework, essentially showing the latents of differently generated synthetic data and comparing to see which is closer to the real data latent MoG.

    Firstly, we gather synthetic data from three sources that attempt to mimic the real data behaviours. Specifically RVO, CCP, and MPACT [3, 1, 4]; for more details on the respective simulators/methods, please refer to the supplementary material. The parameters for RVO are set to match the real data, whereas CCP denotes the behaviour produced when manually setting a single CCP profile that best matches the real data by inspection (both reported in [4]). The latter, modCCP, refers to the modCCP behaviour profiles inferred and optimised through the MPACT model. Henceforth, we refer to the optimised modCCP weights as MPACT, for consistency and readability; other references to modCCP imply controlled profiles of the simulator itself - not optimised by the MPACT model. Therefore, we expect that our metric based on MoG latent distributions, is better for MPACT trajectories.

    Each set of simulator-specific trajectories is passed though our pipeline and juxtaposed against the real latents. Then, a new posterior distribution can be defined according to the new clustering, and is compared to the original. Figure 7 demonstrates the plotted latents for each inference dataset. Figure 7 also shows the visualisations per-simulator, along with the new distribution means. From the figures, we can observe that the MPACT latents are closest to the real ones, while RVO values tend to be confined and not access the whole latent space. This could be due to the limited behavioural variability of the simulator itself, since its target use is for generating local movements. We also calculate the metric introduced in Section IV-C between the pairs of real and simulated cluster centres (Table IV). The averaged metric value is lower for MPACT-predicted trajectories, confirming our expectations.

    The method is generalisable, and so we can input additional simulator-specific data (Figure 8) that mimic the real behaviours, specifically from CEDRL [16], GREIL [6], and PAG [10]. We can see that the CEDRL distribution is close to the real ones, yielding a latent metric of 2.006, placing it second best after MPACT (1.867). We can also restrict the data we use to a single scene, e.g., Zara, and plot the Zara-generated data for GREIL and PAG to assess their embeddings when focusing on a specific scenario. Both graphically and according to the latent metric, GREIL outperforms PAG (latent difference ≈.5), which makes sense since GREIL is a more recent method, trained on real data with inverse RL and is consistent with observations made in the original paper ([6]). GREIL was trained on three datasets, namely “Chat and Flock-1” [7], and Flock and Zara. For new datasets it requires a separate trained policy.

    Overall, users can utilise this framework by directly inputting a set of trajectories which simulates the real scenarios (e.g., church yard, commercial street, university campus) and observe how close they are to the real data features, qualitatively, by visualising the posterior distributions and cluster means in the learned embedding space, or quantitatively, by calculating a latent metric. Users can also sample the learned space to inspect generated trajectories.

    V-BEmbedding Space Coverage

    We can also use the model on data that do not simulate the real scenarios. In that case, the model is used as a way to visualise how spread the inputs are in the embedding space.

    For instance, inputting only goal, group and interaction-specific behaviours from modCCP weights (e.g., {w_g=1,w_gr=0,wᵢ=0}), as shown in Figure 12, shows how well the simulator’s principal behaviours can cover the real behaviour space. We remind that this experiment references modCCP and not MPACT, since the profiles used are controlled (principal behaviours), and not optimised by the MPACT model. From Figure 12, it can be seen that the grouping and interaction behaviours have major overlap in the embedding space, which is expected since the dynamics are similar, with the main difference being in the environment context (proximity to POIs). We observe then that these principal behaviours alone, do not span the range of the real behaviours, and so a mixture of them is necessary for obtaining a dataset that can be used, for example, for training models on synthetic data.

    Another functionality of our embedding is testing the data projected far from the learned distribution. It is interesting to consider trajectories from a controlled environment, e.g., people instructed to follow a single line [45, 46], which is rare to find in in-the-wild data. Figure 9 shows that indeed the embeddings are outside of the learned MoG, and also shows that they are clustered together which is expected since this corridor scenario “forces” behaviours to be very similar.

    An additional example of embeddings projected outside the MoG is depicted in Figure 10, where bike trajectories were captured in a constrained environment [47, 48] (data from a project funded by the German Science Foundation (DFG) under DFG-Grant No. KL 1873/1-1 and SE 1789/1-1.). We can also observe the effect of increasing the amount of cyclists in this confined setup, revealing in both instances that the inferred latents fall outside the learned distribution, as expected; not only this oval pattern is rare in natural movements, but the speed differences also affect the perceived behaviours. For additional results, refer to the supplementary material.

    V-CGuiding the Generations

    Provided the posterior distribution of the real data, and a corresponding empirical distribution based on data from a specific simulator, e.g., MPACT [4], we can further explore the functionalities of our system by editing the observed distribution. Figure 11 shows an example of editing the MPACT distribution, specifically shifting one of its inferred cluster centres to coincide with that of the real data. Since the PCA operation is reversible, we can inspect the latent space visualisation (in 2D) and edit accordingly. Then, the new informed distribution incorporates the new cluster mean, and so we can sample from it (with the unedited cluster’s frequency and covariance), as shown in Figure 11-right. The latent space “trajeform” metric, decreases from 1.867 (as reported in Table IV) to 1.254, implying that visually editing the observed latents to have bigger overlap with the trained latents, translates into higher distribution similarity with the real data.

    Since operating on the learned space yields meaningful outcomes, we can then use our model to “guide” the selection of parameters in a different parameter space, say p∈ℙ, to create a parameter set that is balanced subject to the real data profiles. For this use case, we set ℙ∈ℝ⁴ to be modCCP profile space. We remind that modCCP is a simulator that has been used to create the synthetic data to train MPACT - a parameter prediction model. To collect the training data, one could simply randomly sample the parameter space (Figure 14-d). However, the real data do not often span the whole space as can be seen from Figure 13-taken directly from the original MPACT paper [4]. Note here, that for our visualisations we use the same format as MPACT, for uniformity, i.e., converting the goal, group and interaction weights (which sum up to 1) to barycentric coordinates, and denote the connectivity weight (from 0 to 1) via marker size.

    Now, with our model, we can sample our posterior distribution as in Figure 14-a. Then, we can estimate a mapping M:ℤ→ℙ. One way to do this is via nearest neighbour search: since we have the ground truth weights of the modCCP trajectories passed through our model, we can find the cluster centres in ℙ, and tune accordingly, as in Figure 14-b. We could also learn a simple MLP (Multi-Layer Perceptron) parameter model to predict this mapping, and tune as in Figure 14-c. The parameter model is trained on mean square error loss, on data created by passing modCCP generation (with known weights) through our encoder, and getting the corresponding latents in ℤ; the model yields training and validation losses 0.0484 and 0.0499, respectively, after 200 epochs. We can see that in both cases the tuned points adhere by the real data coverage of ℙ, more than the random sampling. Still, it is important to note a few important considerations. The plotted points in Figure 13, taken from the original paper, correspond to profiles per area and per frame-window. In our case, the points correspond to the trajectories, as these are preprocessed by our block, hence there are some discrepancies between the two patterns. A user can trade-off the limited predictive capability of the MLP parameter model with the reliability of nearest neighbours, according to the intended application.

    VI Evaluation

    VI-ASelf-Consistency Check

    Prior to the qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we perform a sanity-check experiment to verify the robustness of the learned embedding space. More specifically, we assess whether sampling latent vectors according to the learned MoG distribution, decoding them into trajectory space, and subsequently re-projecting the generated trajectories back into the latent space through the encoder, results in latent points that still adhere to the learned MoG distribution (Figure 15). For sampling, we use 2k points to match the size of the training dataset. From Figure 15, we confirm both visually and quantitatively, through the obtained metric value of .705 (<1), that the learned latent space is self-consistent.

    VI-BAssessment Premise

    Our aim in this evaluation is to investigate two claims, (i) that following the guidance of our learned latent distribution gives an advantage over no guidance for generation, and (ii) our model encodes information tailored to the real data. Hence, in order to determine the evaluation framework, we discuss each claim and reach a comparison objective that will provide evidence for our claims.

    For (i), we use an existing set of trajectories, tₕ, say from simulator, h. We compute z_R,zₕ via z=E_θ(τ), and sample ℤ to get z_G, where the distribution of our posterior (G) is closer to the real latents than the distribution of zₕ (e.g., just the sampled prior). Then we use the trained decoder D_θ:ℤ→T to get decoded τ_G,S, where τ_S the decoded version of τₕ. Finally we compare τ_G and τ_S, aiming to prove that the trajectories with latents more faithful to the distribution of z_R, are closer to the real trajectories, than the other latents. We use both CCP baseline and the prior as the sampled distributions, and so, we compare the generated trajectories from our posterior, the prior, and the CCP empirical distribution.

    For (ii), let there be E^′ an alternative encoder, e.g., MPACT, then, p_R=E^′(τ_R). We sample from the distribution of p_R to get p_G. We obtain τ^′_G via a known decoder D^′. We compare our obtained τ_G and τ^′_G to the real data. In practice this essentially means comparing the trajectories decoded from two latent distributions: our inferred MoG (τ_G), and the distribution of the observed embeddings of another parameter space, MPACT (τ^′_G).

    Thus, we compare our posterior with MPACT (ii), prior and other simulators (i). We emphasise that all comparisons are made between trajectories generated through our decoder, to ensure that we do not inherently compare simulator specifics, but the embeddings of these simulated data against the real.

    VI-CQuantitative Assessment

    In order to quantify “closeness” to the real data, we sample the latent distributions of five sources, i.e., prior, inferred MoG, RVO, CCP baseline, and MPACT. We compute three types of metrics on trajectories from our decoder for comparison fairness; we want to exclude accumulated limitations of different simulators. So, for each source, we sample their distributions to obtain a set of trajectories and compare them with the real ground truths. Specifically, we calculate: (a) our latent metric described in Section IV-C, (b) the Maximum Mean Discrepancy-MMD [49] values (statistical measure for comparing distributions), (c) Sliced Wasserstein Distance [50] (SWD), and (d) the energy distance of each set of generated data against the real data. We use SWD because we do not have 1-1 matching of trajectories and want to measure them containing similar behaviours. SWD measures the similarity between two distributions by comparing their projections along multiple random 1D directions and averaging the resulting Wasserstein distances. The energy distance is a direct distributional distance between two unpaired sets, like MMD, but does not require choosing a kernel. We finally calculate (e) the Jensen-Shannon Divergence-JSD (symmetric and stable measure for comparing probability distributions): for trajectory features (x/z positions and speeds) and other additional trajectory-based behaviour measures (Deviation From Goal-DFG and Movement Direction Diversity-MDD). We report these values in Table IV.

    From Table IV we can see that the MoG distribution is closest to the real data in the majority of the metrics, outperforming the prior and MPACT, and so providing evidence for our claims (i) and (ii). Additionally, MPACT achieves overall better scores among the simulator sources, with RVO being second best. We can also see that our metric follows the emergent “trends” of the other established metrics, i.e, the ranking of the “best” sources is consistent. The energy distance ranks CCP second best, which again reveals that different metrics focus on different aspects. Hence, some discrepancies between metrics appear, which is sensible since different metrics often assess different aspects of behaviours/simulations. Therefore, the goal is not to replace existing metrics, but to introduce an additional measure that captures complementary aspects of behavioural similarity.

    Further contextualising the results, Table V reports an extra set of metrics that operate on the latent space (apart from our latent metric): latent energy, and MoG Wasserstein Distance. Fréchet Distance [51] measures the similarity between two trajectories by quantifying the minimum maximum distance required to traverse both paths while preserving their point ordering. We refrain from using Fréchet Distance on the trajectory space since it becomes extremely slow, and instead, we calculate it on the “core” trajectories found from each inference run, and report the ranking in decreasing order: MPACT, RVO, and CCP. Latent energy and MoG WD ranking coincide with that of the latent metric. Overall, the ranking trends provide additional evidence for the quantitative evaluation.

    VI-DQualitative Assessment

    Next, we visualise some of the aforementioned results, for qualitative inspection. Figure 17 shows the heatmaps illustrating the difference in the correlation matrices of real and generated data, for four sets of generated data, each associated with a different empirical latent distribution. Correlation matrices [52] are built by computing trajectory features, i.e., positions x and z, speed, acceleration and angular difference, to find whether correlations and dependencies between features are preserved. Taking the difference from the real data matrix, assess representativeness to the real data features. We observe that our posterior returns the smallest differences with MPACT being a close second. Finally, we plot boxplots of the trajectory features (positions and speed) of the real data, and the four sources (excluding the prior) in Figure 16, showing that our MoG posterior and the MPACT generations are closer to the real data, confirming the quantitative assessment observations.

    VII Discussion

    In this work, we learn an encoding that yields a latent representation, embedding real data features, thus parameterising trajectory information. To do this, we utilised trajectories captured in real life to train a VAE on the task of trajectory reconstruction. We use the trained model encoder to build a posterior distribution (MoG) based on the observed data (latents of the real data), according to predicted cluster centres (k-means clustering). Then we employ our method for embedding synthetic data from various simulators to measure latent distribution similarity. The feature space is aligned with the real one, enabling comparisons between the two sets of latent distributions. We can then inform the selection of latents, and guide it towards a distribution of choice. This functionality enables measuring behaviour fidelity in an aligned embedding space which is useful for comparing synthetic data to real, as well as for assessing whether new training datasets contain behavioural features that adhere to those of the real ones.

    Limitations and Future Work

    Despite the new opportunities that our method offers, it has some limitations. Our model does not take into account environmental information explicitly, e.g., POIs, in its inputs, which limits our system’s ability to assign specific semantic meaning to the latent space, e.g., action labels. Also, it does not directly receive information regarding neighbouring actions and group behaviours. But, these actions are implicitly entangled into the input trajectories, since it falls upon the simulator to produce paths that mimic the real ones, including the spawns and densities of agents. Still, it would be beneficial to further experiment with such aspects in the input representation which, however, would require more data since the task becomes more difficult.

    Additionally, the amount of real data is limited and so the model cannot capture the full range of behavioural features that could emerge. The absence of a large corpus of tracked trajectories captured in-the-wild affects both the encoding power and choice of architecture. Experimenting with more advanced model architectures, e.g., transformers, would be interesting, which entails the creation of a larger training database of real trajectories. Finally, our method is not extensively assessed against a large variety of alternative quantitative and qualitative metrics, an analysis that would reveal both its strengths and weaknesses. However, the lack of baseline state-of-the-art scores, benchmark evaluation metrics and tasks, makes the proper formulation of such a protocol an interesting but challenging direction for future work.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 400 万粒子跑 140 帧：用 Compute Shader 在 Unity 里实现完整 FLIP 流体，一次 MGPCG 求解 7ms ｜ Compute Shader实现大规模FLIP流体模拟
item.category: 公众号·游戏开发技术教程
item.description:
一句话：256×128×128 网格 + 400 万粒子，RTX 4070 上约 7ms/帧；重点是实现而不是公式。

要点：

  • 选择 FLIP（Fluid-Implicit-Particle）的理由讲清楚了：拉格朗日粒子携带质量与速度随流体运动，避开对流项的网格插值扩散；欧拉网格只负责压力求解，结构规则因此容易上 MGPCG
  • 实现口径很具体：Unity + Compute Shader，模拟规模 400 万粒子 / 400 万网格（256×128×128），一次 MGPCG 求解，RTX 4070 上约 140 FPS、单帧约 7ms
  • 工程约束也交代了：需开启 DX12、仅 N 卡可跑、wrap 线程数 32，作者注明只在自己的 4070 上测过——属于「能跑的样例」而不是通用库

为什么值得看：FLIP 在中文技术圈几乎没有完整实现可参考，这篇把「粒子 + 网格 + MGPCG」这条链路在 Unity 里走通了，并给了可对照的性能口径。做水体、泥浆、软体耦合的团队可以直接拿它的规模与帧时间当基线。

中文摘要：一篇填补空白的实现向长文：作者指出中文圈里 Stable Fluid 的 NS 方法与 SPH/PBF 粒子都有大量文章，唯独经典 FLIP 没多少人写，于是自己在 Unity 里用 Compute Shader 实现了一套。文章重点放在实现而非公式推导：FLIP 把拉格朗日粒子与欧拉网格结合，粒子携带质量与速度并跟随流体运动，从而避免对流项里网格插值造成的数值扩散，也能免追踪液面就表达自由表面；网格只负责压力求解，因为结构规则，MGPCG 这类求解器容易跑起来。实测规模是 400 万粒子配 400 万网格（256×128×128），一次 MGPCG 求解，在 RTX 4070 上约 140 帧、单帧约 7ms；工程限制也写得很实在——需要 DX12、目前只测过 N 卡。

主题：图形学

来源：公众号·游戏开发技术教程（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-14

本期推送：2026-11-02

写在前面

知乎上有很多Stable Fluid的NS流体和SPH/PBF方法的粒子流体，但是作为经典流体模拟方法的FLIP方法竟然没什么人写，填补一下这个空白。由于本人只是业余流体爱好者，故本文不详细解释公式推导，重点着眼于实现，

下面是我在Unity中使用Compute shader实现的FLIP流体模拟，使用一次MGPCG求解，模拟规模为400w粒子和400w网格（256x128x128），在RTX4070上以140帧左右运行，耗时约7ms。

工程链接如下（需要开启DX12，且目前仅能在Nvidia显卡上运行，（wrap线程数为32）编写时未考虑其他型号，且只在我的RTX4070上测试过）

[1]

简介

FLIP (Fluid-Implicit-Particle) 是一种用于流体模拟的混合欧拉-拉格朗日算法。该算法将拉格朗日粒子与欧拉网格相结合，其中粒子携带质量、速度等物理属性并跟随流体运动，从而避免了对流项中网格插值带来的数值扩散问题，同时无需追踪液面即可方便地模拟自由表面流体。网格则负责压力求解，由于网格结构规则，计算过程大为简化，且易于实现 MGPCG 这类高效求解器。

相较于传统纯网格方法，FLIP 解决了对流项计算产生的数值耗散问题；相较于纯粒子方法，FLIP 求解简单、具备欧拉方法的稳定性，同时保持了流体计算的稳定性和高效性。

整个算法大致分为三个步骤：

第一步：粒子到网格

模拟开始时，每个粒子携带着各自的速度和位置信息。首先，需要将这些离散粒子的信息传递到固定的背景网格上。通过插值，每个网格节点获得由周围粒子贡献的加权平均速度。这一步构建了粒子与网格之间的桥梁，为后续计算准备数据。

第二步：网格上求解

此时，所有流体运动数据均已汇集到网格上。在网格层面求解纳维-斯托克斯方程的核心部分——压力投影，目标是计算出一组压力值，使流体在满足不可压缩性条件的同时产生恰当的流动。网格的优势在于，此阶段可以使用高效、成熟的数值方法（如预处理共轭梯度法）求解压力泊松方程，从而确保整体稳定性。

第三步：网格回粒子

求解完成后，得到新的网格速度场，需要将这些变化“反馈”给粒子。与 PIC (Particle-In-Cell) 方法相比，FLIP 的核心做法是：计算求解前后网格速度的变化量（即速度增量），然后将该增量叠加到粒子的原有速度上。由于这种做法会产生误差累积导致的噪声，实际应用中通常采用 FLIP 与 PIC 的混合速度更新方式，例如常用的 FLIP 95 即为 5% PIC 与 95% FLIP 的混合比例。

FLIP 算法的两大核心组成部分是网格上的求解以及粒子与网格之间的信息传递，下面将分别进行讲解。

压力求解

我们需要在网格上求解压力泊松方程（此处推导过程略）：

使用交错网格（MAC网格，Marker-and-Cell / Staggered Grid），

压力 p：存储在网格中心

速度 u/v：存储在网格面中心（x方向速度在左侧面中心，y方向速度在下侧面中心）

其中：

：网格单元左边界上的水平速度 ：网格单元右边界上的水平速度 ：网格单元下边界上的垂直速度 ：网格单元上边界上的垂直速度

每个单元存储左面     和下面     （三维场景还需存储后面）的速度分量，以及中心点的压力/散度。

在二维MAC网格上，网格单元 (i, j) 的散度计算方式为：

将模拟区域的边界视作固体边界，速度为0，代码实现非常简单：

float3 vel = GridVelocity[i]; float v_xn = coord.x + 1 < GridSize.x ? GridVelocity[Coord2Idx(cellIdx + uint3(1, 0, 0))].x : 0; float v_yn = coord.y + 1 < GridSize.y ? GridVelocity[Coord2Idx(cellIdx + uint3(0, 1, 0))].y : 0; float v_zn = coord.z + 1 < GridSize.z ? GridVelocity[Coord2Idx(cellIdx + uint3(0, 0, 1))].z : 0; float divergence = InvCellSize * (v_xn - vel.x + v_yn - vel.y + v_zn - vel.z);

对于网格单元 (i, j)，压力拉普拉斯算子离散化为：

由于一般采用正方形网格，可以简化为

离散后的二维压力泊松方程为：

显然，这是一个对称正定（SPD）的线性方程组      。

我们先确定固体的单元格，然后将包含粒子的视为液体单元格，其余为空气单元。

对于固体边界，我们将与边界相邻的面的速度分量设为0，即Neumann边界。

对于自由表面，由于我们这里模拟单相流，将大气压设为0，即Dirichlet边界。

uint gridType = GridTypes[index]; uint2 xAxisType = NeighborGridTypeAxis(0, gridType); uint2 yAxisType = NeighborGridTypeAxis(1, gridType); uint2 zAxisType = NeighborGridTypeAxis(2, gridType);                  float center = 6; if (IsSolidCell(xAxisType.x)) center -= 1; if (IsSolidCell(xAxisType.y)) center -= 1; if (IsSolidCell(yAxisType.x)) center -= 1; if (IsSolidCell(yAxisType.y)) center -= 1; if (IsSolidCell(zAxisType.x)) center -= 1; if (IsSolidCell(zAxisType.y)) center -= 1;                  float4 a = 0; if (IsFluidCell(gridType))     a = float4(center,                 IsFluidCell(xAxisType.x) ? -1 : 0,                 IsFluidCell(yAxisType.x) ? -1 : 0,                 IsFluidCell(zAxisType.x) ? -1 : 0);                  _A[index] = a;

最简单直接的求解方法当然是雅可比方法或者红黑高斯赛德尔方法迭代求解，但是收敛非常之慢，虽说少量迭代也能凑合用，但是几十次迭代的耗时已经超过了MGPCG方法的耗时，并且残差更大。

对于压力泊松方程，既然系数矩阵A是对称正定的，可以使用共轭梯度法求解，然而，单纯的共轭梯度方法收敛同样很慢，其收敛速度严重依赖矩阵条件数，在高分辨率条件下迭代次数会急剧增加。

为了提高收敛速度，可以使用预处理共轭梯度法（PCG），需要找到一个预处理矩阵M，使得      的条件数远小于A。应用预处理后，实际求解的方程是     ，由于     的条件数远小于A本身，共轭梯度方法可以快速收敛。

我们通常采用多重网格（Multigrid）方法作为预处理器。虽然多重网格本身也可以作为求解器，但对于病态问题可能不够稳定。

MGPCG (Multigrid Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient) 是一种将多重网格法作为预处理器与共轭梯度法相结合的迭代求解器。简单来说，它的核心思路是：用多重网格法对原方程进行预处理，降低方程的条件数，再用共轭梯度法在这个预处理后的方程上迭代。这种方法既继承了多重网格法收敛速度与网格规模无关的优点，又利用了共轭梯度法的稳健性，特别适合处理流体模拟中的压力泊松方程这类大规模稀疏线性系统。MGPCG 将多重网格作为 PCG 的预处理子，实现了“1+1>2”的效果：MG方法负责处理高频误差和全局耦合，CG方法负责保证稳健收敛。

多重网格方法的实现

由于雅可比或者高斯赛德尔等迭代方法只有局部信息的传递。高频误差可以通过局部邻居信息快速平均掉，但低频误差（长波分量）需要信息在整个区域传播，这需要大量迭代。

因此多重网格将这些方法作为光滑器，简单迭代数次消除高频误差后，通过限制算子将细网格的残差传递到粗网格，原先高分辨率上的相对低频误差在粗网格上又变成高频，经过不断地光滑和粗化，直到网格分辨率小到可以快速求解，之后再逐层向下将粗网格的修正量传递回细网格。

整个流程如下：

由于我们将多重网格方法作为共轭梯度法的预处理器，因此需要小心保持矩阵的对称性，这里采用红黑高斯赛德尔方法作为光滑器，论文指出最佳迭代次数为3，预平滑和后平滑需要相同的迭代次数，如果预平滑采用 红-黑-红-黑 的顺序，则后平滑需要 黑-红-黑-红 的迭代顺序。

for (int i = 0; i < top; i++) {     int res = GridRes >> i;     PreSmooth(As[i], Zs[i], Rs[i], res, 3);     Restriction(Rs[i], As[i], Zs[i], Rs[i + 1], As[i + 1], Zs[i+1], res); }  SymmetricGaussSeidel(Rs[top], As[top], Zs[top], GridRes >> top, 4);  for (int i = top - 1; i >= 0; i--) {     int res = GridRes >> i;     Prolongation(Zs[i+1], Zs[i], As[i], res);     PostSmooth(As[i], Zs[i], Rs[i], res, 3); }

除了红黑高斯赛德尔方法之外，还可以采用阻尼雅可比，或者更优的 Scheduled Relaxed Jacobi (SRJ)，此处不再赘述。

此外，普通的多重网格法只在粗网格上求解残差，并将修正量传递回细网格，对于自适应精度网格，由于结构本身具有多级精度，因此需要在粗网格上求解原方程，粗化时不仅要粗化残差，还需要粗化细网格上的解。

非平滑聚合代数多重网格（UAAMG）

由于现在UAAMG似乎已经成为规则的笛卡尔网格上流体求解的标配，本文也采用它来作为我们的预处理器。原论文链接：

A Fast Unsmoothed Aggregation Algebraic Multigrid Framework for the Large-Scale Simulation of Incompressible Flow[2]

在粗化过程中，我们需要计算单元中的残差，限制到粗网格上（u为当前解）：

在UAAMG中，粗化时不仅要限制残差，还要粗化泊松系数，由于系数对称，每个网格单元只存储对角线系数和上三角（或下三角）矩阵的非对角线系数。

粗网格内部细网格节点的连接系数，部分连接在内部四个节点之间，部分连接到相邻的网格节点，需要分别累加。粗化后，粗网格矩阵通过伽辽金原理      得到，对于泊松方程，该操作等价于对系数进行加权平均。

以二维液体内部为例，每个细网格上的单元的对角线系数为4，非对角线系数都是-1，粗网格包含四个细网格。将内部和外部系数分别求和然后乘以1/4，得到粗网格上的对角线系数为 2，非对角线系数为 -0.5 。

论文给出的粗化伪代码如下。由于我们仅存储一半的非对角线系数，所以遇到内部的非对角线系数时要算两次。

我的实现代码如下：

float rCoarse = 0; float4 aCoarse = 0; for (int zz = 0; zz < 2; zz++) for (int yy = 0; yy < 2; yy++) for (int xx = 0; xx < 2; xx++) {     int fx = x * 2 + xx;     int fy = y * 2 + yy;     int fz = z * 2 + zz;     int fi = Coord2Index(fx, fy, fz, gridResF);     float4 aFine = _aFine[fi];     if (!IsFluidCell(aFine))         continue;     aCoarse.x += aFine.x;     float sum = NeighborSum(_aFine, _vFine, aFine, fx, fy, fz, gridResF);     float rFine = _fFine[fi] - _ih2 * (aFine.x * _vFine[fi] + sum);     rCoarse += rFine;          if (xx == 0) aCoarse.y += aFine.y;     else aCoarse.x += aFine.y * 2;                          if (yy == 0) aCoarse.z += aFine.z;     else aCoarse.x += aFine.z * 2;                          if (zz == 0) aCoarse.w += aFine.w;     else aCoarse.x += aFine.w * 2; }  _rCoarse[ci] = rCoarse * 0.125f; _aCoarse[ci] = aCoarse * 0.125f; _eCoarse[ci] = 0;

在粗网格上求解残差之后需要将修正值插值回细网格：

注意这里有一个系数      ，论文指出，当 UAAMG 用作预条件子时，对泊松方程设置      = 2可以改善收敛性。原因是：通过伽辽金原理和分片常数插值得到的粗网格矩阵，往往会将误差修正量低估大约一半。即在插值步骤将粗网格上的修正量加回细网格时乘上      = 2，可以加速收敛。然而，当 UAAMG 作为独立的迭代求解器而非预条件器使用时可能导致不收敛，应该设置      = 1以避免过度修正和不稳定性。

这里我实际测试了一下确实如此，不过由于我们使用UAAMG作为预条件器，采用      =2以获得更快的收敛速度。

float4 ac = _aFine[fi]; if (!IsFluidCell(ac)) return; int cx = fx >> 1; int cy = fy >> 1; int cz = fz >> 1; _eFine[fi] += _eCoarse[Coord2Index(cx, cy, cz, gridResC)] * 2;

使用预条件器的共轭梯度法伪代码如下：

代码实现如下：

Dot(R, Z, rz_old); if (abs(rz_old.Value) > 1e-5f) {     for (int iter = 0; iter < maxIter; iter++)     {         Laplace(A, P, Ap, GridRes, H);         Dot(P, Ap, pAp);         UpdateVR(P, Ap, V, R, rz_old, pAp);          if (iter == maxIter - 1) break;                              MultiGridVCycle();         Dot(R, Z, rz_new);         UpdateP(Z, P, rz_old, rz_new);          (rz_old, rz_new) = (rz_new, rz_old);     } }

我这里采用一次MGPCG求解，不需要进入下一次循环，因此省掉步骤5及步骤7之后的步骤直接结束，实际测试表明一次MGPCG迭代求解效果已经远优于几十次雅可比或者红黑高斯-赛德尔迭代，求解耗时仅需1.5ms，

粒子和网格的信息传递 P2G

该步骤的目标是：将离散粒子的动量（质量×速度）汇聚到固定的背景网格节点上，为在网格上求解压力方程准备一个速度场。通过P2G，我们将混乱的粒子数据映射到了一个规则可控的网格环境中。

在FLIP中，我们通常不会直接传递速度，而是传递动量。因为只插值速度会破坏动量守恒。

是基于粒子位置和网格节点距离的插值权重。在FLIP中，通常使用B样条（B-Spline）基函数（特别是二次或三次B样条）作为插值核。 Linear B-Spline Kernels：

Quadratic B-Spline Kernels:

P2G 的实现通常有 Splat 和 Gather 两种方式，分别对应粒子写入影响范围内的网格和网格收集周围粒子。无论采用哪种方式，都需要对粒子进行排序，使相同单元格中的粒子聚集在一起优化访问。本文采用粒子所在网格索引作为键进行排序，由于键为正整数，直接使用基数排序（Radix Sort）实现，算法实现可参考我之前的文章：

【UnityShader】GPU排序的简单实现（Radix Sort)[3]

或者是视频：

[4]

由于粒子数量小于2^24，所以排序仅进行三轮处理24bit，然后将粒子按照排序后的位置重新排列，整个过程耗时大概1.5ms

Gather

gather方法实现非常简单，直接每个线程一个单元格，获取周围3x3x3的单元格的粒子，累加xyz面上的动量和质量，最后相除得到网格上的速度。

Splat

Splat 方法相对复杂。首先，一个线程组处理 8×8×8的块，因此需预先计算整个块的粒子索引范围。由于网格索引使用莫顿码，直接取整个块范围的最大最小值即可。8×8×8块的粒子会影响 10×10×10 范围的单元格，每个单元格需累加xyz方向的速度和质量以及网格中心的质量，因此需要长度为 1000×7的共享数组。先将粒子 splat 到共享数组中，之后再累加到全局以减少冲突。

由于 HLSL 不支持浮点数原子累加操作，这里声明 int 数组。这里参考这篇论文中给出的代码实现：

Cirrus: Adaptive Hybrid Particle-Grid Flow Maps on GPU[5]

该方法利用 Wave Instincts 进一步减小块内写入共享内存时的冲突。由于粒子已事先按网格键排序，先由每个线程访问前一个线程粒子的键，若与本线程不同，说明该线程是一段相同单元格粒子的起始边界。之后计算最大区间长度，分别累加每个区间内的粒子的各项属性，最后由起始位置的粒子的线程写入共享内存，从而大幅减少块内线程写入共享内存时的冲突。

该方法需要所有粒子splat完成之后，重新Dispatch一个pass将每个单元的动量除以质量得到单元格的各个面的速度分量。

float3 pos = DecodePosition(p.packedPosition); float3 vel = DecodeVelocity(p.packedVelocity);  int3 pCoord = PositionCoord(p.packedPosition); int3 localCoord = pCoord - coordMin; int laneid = WaveGetLaneIndex(); int local_idx = LocalIdx(localCoord); bool is_boundary = WaveIsFirstLane(); if (!is_boundary) { int prev_idx = WaveReadLaneAt(local_idx, laneid - 1); is_boundary = prev_idx != local_idx; } uint mark = reversebits(WaveActiveBallot(is_boundary)); uint chk = laneid < 31 ? ((mark << (laneid + 1)) | ((1U << (laneid + 1)) - 1)) : 0xFFFFFFFF; int interval = 31 - asint(firstbithigh(chk));  // 从当前线程开始的连续 0 数量 int iter = WaveActiveMax(interval);  for (int offi = -1; offi <= 1; ++offi) for (int offj = -1; offj <= 1; ++offj) for (int offk = -1; offk <= 1; ++offk)  { int3 neighborCoord = pCoord + int3(offi, offj, offk);   float3 cellCenter = (neighborCoord + 0.5f) * _CellSize; float3 position_vx = cellCenter + float3(-0.5f * _CellSize, 0, 0); float3 position_vy = cellCenter + float3(0, -0.5f * _CellSize, 0); float3 position_vz = cellCenter + float3(0, 0, -0.5f * _CellSize);   float3 weights = float3( GetWeight(pos, position_vx, _InvCellSize), GetWeight(pos, position_vy, _InvCellSize), GetWeight(pos, position_vz, _InvCellSize));   float3 warp_velocity_sum = weights * vel; float3 warp_weight_sum = weights; float3 vec = pos - cellCenter; float density = SmoothingKernelPoly6(dot(vec, vec) * _InvCellSize * _InvCellSize);   int stride = 1; while (stride <= iter)   { float3 neighbor_velocity = WaveReadLaneAt(warp_velocity_sum, laneid + stride); float3 neighbor_weights = WaveReadLaneAt(warp_weight_sum, laneid + stride); float3 neighbor_density = WaveReadLaneAt(density, laneid + stride); if (stride <= interval) { warp_velocity_sum += neighbor_velocity; warp_weight_sum += neighbor_weights; density += neighbor_density; }   stride <<= 1; }   int index = LocalIdx(localCoord + int3(offi, offj, offk)); bool is_valid = all(neighborCoord >= 0) && all(neighborCoord < _GridSize) && index >= 0 && index < 1000;   if (is_boundary && is_valid) { InterlockedAdd(g_dataSum[index + 0 * 1000], (int)round(warp_velocity_sum.x * SCALER)); InterlockedAdd(g_dataSum[index + 1 * 1000], (int)round(warp_velocity_sum.y * SCALER)); InterlockedAdd(g_dataSum[index + 2 * 1000], (int)round(warp_velocity_sum.z * SCALER));   InterlockedAdd(g_dataSum[index + 3 * 1000], (int)round(warp_weight_sum.x * SCALER)); InterlockedAdd(g_dataSum[index + 4 * 1000], (int)round(warp_weight_sum.y * SCALER)); InterlockedAdd(g_dataSum[index + 5 * 1000], (int)round(warp_weight_sum.z * SCALER)); InterlockedAdd(g_dataSum[index + 6 * 1000], (int)round(density * SCALER)); } }

不过可能是由于hlsl和CUDA之间的差异，经过反复调整这个方法只比gather方法略快一丢丢，先暂且放着吧。

G2P

它的目标是将网格上经过物理计算（主要是压力修正）后的速度变化传递回粒子，更新粒子的速度和位置。

PIC方法：粒子直接覆盖为周围网格速度的加权平均。这种方法非常稳定，但每一次传递都是一次低通滤波，会导致严重的数值耗散（涡流会迅速消失，流体显得粘稠）

FLIP方法：粒子不直接接收绝对速度，而是接收速度的增量（Delta）

纯粹的 FLIP 虽然细节丰富，但容易引入高频噪音。在实际代码通常使用PIC/FLIP 混合方法：

混入少量 PIC 的平滑效果来抑制噪音。

之后粒子采样网格上的无散速度场进行移动，为了减小误差通常采用高阶方法，如四阶龙格库塔方法：

float3 k1 = ReadGridFaceBilinear(pos,  GridVelocity); float3 k2 = ReadGridFaceBilinear(pos + 0.5f * DeltaTime * k1, GridVelocity); float3 k3 = ReadGridFaceBilinear(pos + 0.5f * DeltaTime * k2, GridVelocity); float3 k4 = ReadGridFaceBilinear(pos + DeltaTime * k3, GridVelocity); velocity = (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4) / 6.0f;

当然我们还可以选择添加APIC方法，让粒子额外携带一个Affine矩阵以更精确地实现粒子与网格之间的数据传递，这个算法我没有在GPU实现，贴出二维版的C#代码如下以供参考：

首先在P2G阶段，我们借助Affine矩阵更准确地传递粒子的速度

float2 cellCenter = ((float2)coord + 0.5f) * CellSize; float2 velocity = float2.zero; float2 sum = 0; float density = 0; float2 position_vx = cellCenter + new float2(-0.5f * CellSize, 0.0f); float2 position_vy = cellCenter + new float2(0.0f, -0.5f * CellSize);  for (int x = math.max(coord.x - 2, 0); x <= math.min(coord.x + 1, GridRes - 1); ++x) for (int y = math.max(coord.y - 2, 0); y <= math.min(coord.y + 1, GridRes - 1); ++y) {     var neighborIdx = Coord2Idx(x, y);     int2 range = Range[neighborIdx];     for (int j = range.x; j < range.y; j++)     {         float4 p = ParticlePos[j];         float2 n_x = p.xy;         var n_c = ParticleAffine[j];         var n_v = ParticleVel[j];                                  float2 weight = new float2(             GetWeight(position_vx - n_x, InvCellSize),             GetWeight(position_vy - n_x, InvCellSize));                                  sum += weight;                                  velocity.x += weight.x * (n_v.x + math.mul(n_c, position_vx - n_x).x);         velocity.y += weight.y * (n_v.y + math.mul(n_c, position_vy - n_x).y);                                  float2 dist = n_x - cellCenter;         density += GetPoly6Weight(dist * InvCellSize);     } }  velocity = math.select(float2.zero, velocity / sum, sum > 1e-4f);

在G2P阶段更新Affine矩阵：

int2 coord = GetCoord(pos); float2x2 new_C = float2x2.zero; float2 new_v = float2.zero; float2 old_v = float2.zero;                  for (int x = coord.x - 1; x <= coord.x + 2; ++x) for (int y = coord.y - 1; y <= coord.y + 2; ++y) {     int2 nCoord = new int2(x, y);     int idx = Coord2Idx(math.clamp(nCoord, 0, GridRes - 1));                          float2 g_vel = GridVelocityNew[idx];                          float2 pos_u = (nCoord + new float2(0, 0.5f)) * CellSize;     float2 pos_v = (nCoord + new float2(0.5f, 0)) * CellSize;                          float2 weights = new float2(GetWeight(pos_u - pos, InvCellSize),                         GetWeight(pos_v - pos, InvCellSize));       float2 weightedNewV = weights * g_vel;     float2 weightedOldV = weights * GridVelocityOld[idx];                          float2 dx_u = pos_u - pos;     float2 dx_v = pos_v - pos;      var term = math.float2x2(weightedNewV * new float2(dx_u.x, dx_v.x),                         weightedNewV * new float2(dx_u.y, dx_v.y));                          new_C += term;     new_v += weightedNewV;     old_v += weightedOldV; } 参考链接

[3]【UnityShader】GPU排序的简单实现（Radix Sort) https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/1888596549224858422
